meta.title: Phenomenology of remote sensing from space
meta.subtitle: A source × interaction grid of every established technique, the empty cells, and the concepts that could fill them, with technology readiness per entry
meta.caveat: TRL values are my estimates against NASA definitions, judged for use from space in the stated application, from knowledge through mid-2026 and checked against mission status and the literature on 2026-10-17 and 2026-11-04. They remain hypotheses, and the TRL of a technique is not the TRL of any specific instrument. Every entry now lists the evidence behind its number and the sources for it; markers like {R001} link to the references, which admit only peer-reviewed papers, agency and mission documents, patents and academic books. Items marked verify sit where a scheduled data release or launch will move the number. Novelty claims were the weakest field: of thirteen rated high, one survived a search, and each concept's prior-art field now names what was found.

interactions.label: Reflection
interactions.name: Reflection
interactions.note: Photons leave a surface unchanged in wavelength, in a direction set by surface geometry
interactions.physics: Light returns from an interface without a change of wavelength. The specular component follows the Fresnel equations and the surface slope distribution; the diffuse component is described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF). This grid uses reflection for the geometric-optics regime, where the reflector is much larger than the wavelength, and elastic scattering for particles and volumes whose response depends on the size parameter.
interactions.observable: Spectral radiance as a function of wavelength, view angle and illumination angle; parallax between views.
interactions.yields: Surface composition and condition from spectral reflectance (albedo, vegetation indices, mineral absorption features in the reflected continuum); surface roughness and slicks from the specular component (glint); topography from parallax; change from repeat imaging.
interactions.limit: Needs an illuminator, so the Sun sets the diurnal and seasonal sampling. Atmospheric scattering and absorption must be removed to reach surface reflectance. No information from beneath the first scattering surface. Sensor-sun-target geometry changes the answer, which is why BRDF is a correction for some techniques and the observable for others.

interactions.label: Absorption
interactions.name: Absorption
interactions.note: Photons removed from a beam at wavelengths matching a transition in the medium
interactions.physics: A gas, liquid or solid removes photons at wavelengths matching electronic, vibrational or rotational transitions. Transmission follows Beer–Lambert, T = exp(−τ), with optical depth τ the product of absorber amount and cross-section. Line width carries pressure (Lorentz broadening) and temperature (Doppler broadening); line ratios carry temperature.
interactions.observable: Depth and shape of absorption lines or bands against a known continuum: the solar spectrum, a laser line, thermal emission from below, a star, or lightning.
interactions.yields: Column amounts from line depth; vertical distribution from line shape or from a set of channels with different weighting functions; temperature from line ratios. The O2 A-band at 760 nm serves as an airmass and cloud-height reference because its abundance is known.
interactions.limit: Requires a known background continuum. Spectral resolution must resolve the line relative to its width, which drives instrument size. Strong lines saturate. In cloud and aerosol the photon path length is ambiguous, which converts a scattering problem into an absorption error.

interactions.label: Emission
interactions.name: Emission
interactions.note: The target radiates on its own: thermal, chemiluminescent, electronic, or anthropogenic
interactions.physics: No illuminator is needed. Thermal emission follows the Planck function scaled by emissivity, and in the Rayleigh–Jeans regime (microwave) brightness temperature is linear in physical temperature. Airglow is chemiluminescence from recombination at 85–300 km; aurora is collisional excitation by precipitating particles; lightning is a hot plasma channel; terrestrial gamma-ray flashes are bremsstrahlung; nighttime lights and RF emitters are anthropogenic sources treated here as signals of opportunity.
interactions.observable: Spectral radiance or brightness temperature versus wavelength, view angle and polarization, with no transmitter.
interactions.yields: Surface and atmospheric temperature; emissivity, hence composition; vertical profiles when the emitting gas is also the absorber (sounding); energy deposition (aurora); activity (fires, lights, transmitters); plasma populations (energetic neutral atoms).
interactions.limit: One radiance measurement contains two unknowns, temperature and emissivity, so separation needs multiple bands, angles or a model (split-window, temperature–emissivity separation). Radiometric noise in the microwave scales as T_sys/√(B·t), which fixes dwell and bandwidth. Weak emissions are observable only at night in bands where sunlight competes.

interactions.label: Elastic scattering
interactions.name: Elastic scattering
interactions.note: Photons redirected by particles, density fluctuations or rough surfaces with no change of wavelength
interactions.physics: The regime is set by the size parameter x = 2πr/λ. Rayleigh (x ≪ 1): molecules, intensity ∝ λ⁻⁴, strongly polarized at 90°. Mie (x ~ 1): aerosol and cloud droplets at optical wavelengths, hydrometeors at microwave; the phase function and polarization encode size, shape and refractive index. Geometric and Bragg (x ≫ 1): radar backscatter from surfaces, where resonant Bragg scatter from capillary waves gives the wind signal in scatterometry.
interactions.observable: Scattered intensity as a function of angle, wavelength and polarization; range-resolved when the source is pulsed (lidar, radar).
interactions.yields: Particle size distribution, concentration and phase (aerosol, cloud, precipitation); surface roughness and dielectric constant (radar backscatter); wind over water; vertical structure of cloud and aerosol layers.
interactions.limit: The inverse problem from intensity alone is ill-posed; angle, polarization or multiple wavelengths are needed to separate size from concentration. Multiple scattering in dense media confounds single-scatter retrievals. Attenuation along the path couples the return at depth to everything above it.

interactions.label: Inelastic scattering
interactions.name: Inelastic (fluorescence, Raman, Brillouin, nuclear)
interactions.note: Energy changes in the interaction: fluorescence, Raman, Brillouin, nuclear excitation
interactions.physics: Fluorescence: a photon is absorbed and re-emitted at longer wavelength after internal relaxation; chlorophyll fluoresces at 685 and 740 nm. Raman: a photon scatters with a wavelength shift equal to a vibrational or rotational quantum of the molecule, about 10⁻³ of the elastic cross-section. Brillouin: scattering from thermally excited acoustic waves, shifted by a few GHz in water, set by sound speed. Nuclear: galactic cosmic rays spall nuclei in regolith, which emit characteristic gamma lines and neutrons.
interactions.observable: Emission at a shifted, species-specific wavelength or energy, separable from the elastic return by a filter, etalon or spectrometer.
interactions.yields: Unambiguous species identification (Raman shifts, gamma lines); plant physiological state (solar-induced fluorescence); water temperature (Brillouin shift); elemental abundance and hydrogen content of regolith (gamma and neutron lines).
interactions.limit: Cross-sections are small, so the photon budget decides everything from orbit: Raman is roughly a thousand times weaker than Rayleigh and Brillouin weaker still. Fluorescence needs a pump bright enough to compete with reflected background, which is why solar-induced fluorescence is measured inside Fraunhofer lines where the background is dark.

interactions.label: Refraction & occultation
interactions.name: Refraction & occultation
interactions.note: Ray bending by refractive-index gradients, read along a limb-grazing path
interactions.physics: Refractive index varies with density, water vapor and, at radio frequencies, electron density. A ray grazing the limb bends toward the denser medium; the bending angle as a function of impact parameter inverts (Abel transform) to the refractivity profile. The same geometry gives extinction versus tangent height, differential refraction, and scintillation from turbulence. Ionospheric dispersion delays lower frequencies more, which is how dual-frequency GNSS measures electron content.
interactions.observable: Carrier phase and Doppler of a coherent source behind the limb (GNSS-RO), bending angle, intensity versus tangent height (solar and stellar occultation), scintillation spectrum, differential group delay.
interactions.yields: Refractivity, hence density, pressure and temperature in the stratosphere and upper troposphere; humidity in the lower troposphere given a temperature prior; electron density profiles; turbulence strength; trace gases in occultation.
interactions.limit: Needs a source behind the limb and a receiver in front, so sampling depends on orbital geometry. Vertical resolution is excellent (~100 m) but the measurement averages ~200–300 km along the ray. Temperature and humidity are not separable in the lower troposphere from refractivity alone. Multipath and super-refraction at the boundary layer.

interactions.label: Doppler
interactions.name: Doppler
interactions.note: Frequency shift from relative motion between source, scatterer and receiver
interactions.physics: A reflector moving at radial velocity v_r shifts a monostatic return by Δf = 2v_r/λ; the bistatic form is v·(k̂_s − k̂_i)/λ. Measurement needs a frequency reference narrower than the shift: a coherent local oscillator (heterodyne lidar, radar), a narrow spectral line (airglow, Fraunhofer lines on the Sun), or a received carrier (GNSS, RF emitters for frequency-difference-of-arrival).
interactions.observable: Shift, or spectrum of shifts, of a line or carrier of known rest frequency; for a pulsed system, the Doppler centroid and spectrum of each range gate.
interactions.yields: Wind profiles (lidar, airglow lines); ocean surface currents (along-track interferometry); hydrometeor fall speed and convective motion (Doppler radar); machinery vibration (vibrometry); inter-satellite range rate, hence gravity (GRACE); emitter location (FDOA); helioseismology on the Sun.
interactions.limit: Platform velocity of 7.5 km/s produces shifts far larger than most geophysical signals, so pointing knowledge and orbit knowledge set the floor. The reference must be narrower than the shift, which rules out sunlight reflected from Earth targets. Coherent integration time is bounded by speckle decorrelation.

interactions.label: Polarization
interactions.name: Polarization
interactions.note: Orientation of the field vector, changed by reflection, scattering, emission, or magnetized media
interactions.physics: Reflection polarizes according to the Fresnel coefficients, strongly near Brewster's angle. Rayleigh scattering is fully polarized at 90°; Mie polarization depends on size and shape. Thermal emission from a smooth surface is partially polarized, the complement of its reflectance. In magnetized plasma, Faraday rotation turns the plane of polarization in proportion to electron content times the parallel field; in a magnetic field, spectral lines Zeeman-split into polarized components.
interactions.observable: The Stokes vector (I, Q, U, V) at optical and microwave wavelengths; the full scattering matrix (HH, HV, VH, VV) for polarimetric radar.
interactions.yields: Aerosol size, shape and refractive index; cloud thermodynamic phase; separation of surface roughness from dielectric constant (polarimetric decompositions); ocean wind direction (WindSat); oil and wet surfaces; magnetic field strength (Zeeman, Faraday); ionospheric electron content.
interactions.limit: The polarized fraction of most natural signals is a few percent, so instrument polarization and calibration accuracy dominate the error budget. Optical polarimetry needs three or more analyzer states or a modulator, each costing throughput or time. Faraday rotation is a nuisance for L-band radar unless it is the product.

interactions.label: Phase & coherence
interactions.name: Phase & coherence
interactions.note: Phase of a coherent field against a reference: interferometry, aperture synthesis, correlation
interactions.physics: A coherent field keeps a definite phase relative to a reference. Comparing phase between two apertures (cross-track interferometry, VLBI) or between two passes (repeat-pass InSAR) measures path-length differences to a fraction of a wavelength. Coherently summing returns along a trajectory synthesizes an aperture as long as the path (SAR); cross-correlating many small antennas synthesizes a filled aperture (SMOS). Second-order coherence (intensity correlation) recovers angular structure from photon-arrival statistics without phase-stable optics.
interactions.observable: Interferometric phase modulo 2π, coherence magnitude, fringe visibility, and the complex visibility across a baseline.
interactions.yields: Topography at meter scale (single-pass InSAR); surface deformation at millimeter scale (repeat-pass); three-dimensional structure in canopies and ice (tomography); terrestrial reference frame baselines to millimeters (VLBI); spatial resolution far beyond the physical aperture (SAR, aperture-synthesis radiometry); surface velocity (along-track interferometry).
interactions.limit: Both measurements must be mutually coherent: temporal decorrelation (vegetation, snow, water), atmospheric phase screens, and baseline knowledge all enter directly. Phase is ambiguous modulo 2π, so unwrapping is required. At optical wavelengths the platform must be known to λ/8 (~100 nm) over the synthesis time, which no orbital navigation achieves, so optical aperture synthesis from LEO is physics-dubious without a reference return.

interactions.label: Time of flight & delay
interactions.name: Time of flight & delay
interactions.note: Propagation delay of a pulse or code from a known emission time
interactions.physics: Range follows from delay, R = cΔt/2 for a round trip. A one-way delay works when the clocks are synchronized (GNSS) or the source is periodic and modeled (pulsars). Differential delay between two frequencies isolates dispersive media (ionosphere); differential delay between receivers locates an emitter (time-difference-of-arrival). Photon-counting detectors extend the method to single-photon returns and time-tag each one.
interactions.observable: Round-trip or one-way delay of a pulse, chirp or code; the shape of the returned waveform over a sloped or rough footprint; the arrival-time histogram of single photons.
interactions.yields: Sea-surface height and ocean topography; ice-sheet and land elevation and their change; river and lake levels; precise orbits and the terrestrial reference frame (laser ranging); electron content (dual-frequency delay); emitter geolocation; canopy height and near-shore bathymetry (photon counting).
interactions.limit: Timing precision converts directly to range: 1 ns is 15 cm one-way. Propagation delays in the troposphere and ionosphere must be measured or modeled to the same level. Waveform shape over sloped, rough or vegetated footprints biases the retrieval. Passive time-difference methods need a shared time reference across receivers.

interactions.label: Penetration
interactions.name: Penetration
interactions.note: Radiation entering below the first surface and returning information from depth
interactions.physics: Depth of penetration is set by attenuation. In water it is the diffuse attenuation coefficient, giving tens of meters in clear water for blue-green light. In soil, sand and vegetation the skin depth at radio wavelengths grows as √(λ/σ), so L- and P-band pass through canopy and dry ground where C- and X-band do not. HF and VHF penetrate kilometers of cold ice and dry regolith. Cosmic rays excite the top meter of regolith. Long-period electromagnetic induction reaches the crust and mantle.
interactions.observable: A depth-resolved return from a pulsed sounder, or an integrated signal whose weighting with depth is known (microwave radiometry, satellite-derived bathymetry, neutron albedo).
interactions.yields: Bathymetry; forest biomass and structure; soil moisture in the top centimeters; subsurface layering, paleochannels and buried ice; ice-sheet thickness and basal conditions; regolith composition; crustal and mantle conductivity.
interactions.limit: Longer wavelengths penetrate deeper but need larger antennas and give coarser resolution. Earth's ionosphere reflects below ~10 MHz, which is why radar sounding of Earth's subsurface from orbit is blocked while it works at Mars and the Moon. Conductive or turbid media stop everything at the surface. The surface signal must be separated from the subsurface one.

interactions.label: Field coupling
interactions.name: Field coupling (gravity, magnetic, relativistic)
interactions.note: A field, or a relativistic effect, sensed through its action on a proof mass, atom, clock, plasma, or orbit
interactions.physics: Gravity acts on a proof mass, on an atom in free fall, and on the orbit itself; its gradient is read by comparing two proof masses on a rigid baseline, its variation by ranging between two spacecraft. The magnetic field is read by a fluxgate or by the precession or level splitting of atoms and molecules (Zeeman effect, optically pumped magnetometers) and by Faraday rotation of a traversing wave. Electric fields and plasma are sampled directly. General relativity makes a clock's rate depend on the geopotential, 1.1×10⁻¹⁸ per centimeter of height.
interactions.observable: Acceleration, acceleration gradient, inter-satellite range rate, vector and scalar field magnitude, Zeeman line splitting, polarization rotation, clock frequency, particle cutoff rigidity.
interactions.yields: The geoid and its time variation (groundwater, ice mass, ocean bottom pressure); the core, crustal and ionospheric magnetic fields and the current systems driving them; electron content; geopotential height; radiation-belt and magnetospheric state.
interactions.limit: Field harmonics attenuate with altitude as (R/r)^(n+1), so spatial resolution is tied to orbit height and the lowest useful orbits fight drag. Non-gravitational accelerations must be measured or removed (drag-free control, accelerometers). Internal and external field sources must be separated. A potential field measured above its sources is smooth and non-unique at depth, so there is no image, only an inversion with priors.

evidence.name: Jason-1 (Jason series)
evidence.detail: Continued the TOPEX reference orbit; calibration/validation established continuity of the sea-level record (Jason-2 2008–2019, Jason-3 2016–).

evidence.name: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich
evidence.detail: Operational reference altimeter in the TOPEX/Jason orbit; first reference mission flying delay-Doppler (SAR) mode with interleaved LRM.

evidence.name: CryoSat-2
evidence.detail: First spaceborne delay-Doppler (SAR-mode) and SARIn altimeter; ice-sheet margins and sea-ice freeboard.

techniques.name: Wide-swath interferometric altimetry
techniques.summary: Two antennas on a 10 m boom interferometrically resolve height across a 120 km swath; rivers, lakes, sub-mesoscale ocean.

evidence.name: SWOT
evidence.instrument: KaRIn Ka-band radar interferometer, two antennas on a 10 m mast, 2 x 50 km swaths
evidence.detail: Launched Dec 2022; first wide-swath interferometric altimeter; cm-level water surface elevation over rivers >100 m wide, lakes >250 m x 250 m and sub-mesoscale ocean topography.

techniques.name: Scatterometry
techniques.summary: Backscatter vs azimuth from capillary waves gives ocean-surface wind vectors; also soil moisture and sea-ice type.

evidence.name: Metop ASCAT
evidence.instrument: C-band fan-beam scatterometer, 2 x 550 km swaths
evidence.detail: Operational wind vectors on Metop-A/B/C; also soil moisture and sea-ice products.

evidence.name: QuikSCAT
evidence.instrument: SeaWinds Ku-band pencil-beam scatterometer, 1800 km swath
evidence.detail: Near-real-time ocean wind vectors used operationally in NWP and marine forecasting until antenna spin failure Nov 2009.

evidence.name: CFOSAT
evidence.instrument: SCAT Ku-band rotating fan-beam scatterometer (with SWIM wave spectrometer)
evidence.detail: First rotating fan-beam scatterometer; wind retrievals validated against buoys and ASCAT.

evidence.name: HY-2A (HY-2 series)
evidence.detail: Chinese ocean dynamics series; HY-2A winds evaluated against buoys, ERA-Interim and ASCAT; continued on HY-2B/C/D.

techniques.name: Cloud profiling radar
techniques.summary: Vertical profiles of cloud water and ice; EarthCARE adds Doppler for fall speeds and convective motion.

evidence.name: CloudSat
evidence.instrument: CPR 94 GHz nadir cloud profiling radar
evidence.detail: First spaceborne cloud radar; vertical profiles of cloud water/ice in the A-Train.

evidence.name: EarthCARE
evidence.instrument: CPR 94 GHz Doppler cloud profiling radar (with ATLID, MSI, BBR)
evidence.detail: Launched May 2024; first Doppler cloud radar in space, giving hydrometeor fall speeds and convective vertical motion.

techniques.name: Precipitation radar
techniques.summary: Dual-frequency ratio separates drop size from rain rate; the reference for global precipitation.

evidence.name: TRMM
evidence.detail: First spaceborne precipitation radar; 3-D rain structure in the tropics.

evidence.name: GPM Core Observatory
evidence.instrument: DPR dual-frequency (Ku 13.6 GHz / Ka 35.5 GHz) precipitation radar
evidence.detail: Dual-frequency ratio separates drop-size distribution from rain rate; reference for the global IMERG precipitation product.

techniques.name: Radar sounding of subsurface and ice
techniques.summary: HF/VHF pulses penetrate km of ice and dry regolith; not usable on Earth from orbit because the ionosphere blocks HF.
techniques.trlNote: Mission-proven at Mars and the Moon{R279}{R280}{R281}; not applicable to Earth from orbit.

evidence.name: Mars Express
evidence.detail: Penetrated the polar layered deposits to the base (~3.7 km) and mapped subsurface structure.

evidence.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
evidence.detail: Higher-resolution sounding of polar layered deposits and mid-latitude ice.

evidence.name: JUICE
evidence.detail: Launched Apr 2023; in cruise; designed to sound Ganymede, Europa and Callisto ice shells to ~9 km.

evidence.name: Europa Clipper
evidence.instrument: REASON 9 MHz / 60 MHz dual-frequency ice-penetrating radar
evidence.detail: Launched Oct 2024; in cruise; dual-frequency sounding of Europa's ice shell and near-surface.

evidence.name: Mars Express
evidence.detail: Subsurface radar soundings of Mars polar layered deposits and buried basins.

evidence.name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
evidence.detail: Shallow subsurface sounding of Mars ice and layered deposits.

evidence.name: Kaguya (SELENE)
evidence.detail: Subsurface layers under the nearside maria detected at several hundred metres depth.

techniques.name: Topside ionospheric sounder
techniques.summary: Swept-frequency HF reflects at the plasma frequency; electron-density profiles above the F2 peak.

evidence.name: Alouette 1 / Alouette 2
evidence.instrument: Swept-frequency HF topside sounder (0.5–12 MHz; 0.2–14.5 MHz)
evidence.detail: First topside sounder in orbit (29 Sep 1962); electron-density profiles above the F2 peak from topside ionograms.

evidence.name: ISIS 1 / ISIS 2
evidence.detail: Continued the Alouette programme; ionogram-to-profile reduction established the standard method.

evidence.name: IMAGE
evidence.instrument: RPI Radio Plasma Imager, 3 kHz–3 MHz swept sounder
evidence.detail: Magnetospheric radio sounding from a high-apogee orbit, successor technique to topside sounding.

techniques.name: Photon-counting lidar altimetry
techniques.summary: Single-photon time-tagging at 10 kHz: ice-sheet height change, canopy structure, and incidental bathymetry to ~40 m.

evidence.name: ICESat-2
evidence.instrument: ATLAS 532 nm photon-counting laser altimeter, 6 beams, 10 kHz
evidence.detail: Single-photon time-tagging altimetry; ice-sheet elevation change, sea-ice freeboard, canopy height and demonstrated bathymetry to ~40 m.

evidence.name: GEDI (ISS)
evidence.detail: Full-waveform (not photon-counting) canopy structure and biomass lidar on the ISS; paused 2023–2024 and resumed.

techniques.name: Atmospheric backscatter lidar
techniques.examples: CALIPSO CALIOP, EarthCARE ATLID (HSRL), ACDL (China, HSRL)
techniques.summary: Elastic backscatter profiles aerosol and cloud layers; high-spectral-resolution variants separate molecular from particulate return for absolute extinction.

evidence.name: CALIPSO
evidence.instrument: CALIOP 532/1064 nm dual-polarization elastic backscatter lidar
evidence.detail: 17-year global aerosol and cloud layer profile record; ended Aug 2023.

evidence.name: EarthCARE
evidence.detail: Launched May 2024; HSRL separates molecular and particulate return for direct extinction.

evidence.name: DQ-1 (AEMS)
evidence.instrument: ACDL 532 nm HSRL aerosol channel (plus 1572 nm IPDA)
evidence.operator: CNSA / Ministry of Ecology and Environment, China
evidence.detail: First spaceborne HSRL; initial aerosol retrievals validated against ground lidar networks.

techniques.name: Doppler wind lidar
techniques.summary: Line-of-sight wind from Doppler shift of molecular and aerosol backscatter; the first direct global wind profiles.
techniques.trlNote: Single mission (Aeolus, 2018–2023){R295}{R296}; laser degradation was a known issue{R297}; Aeolus-2 in development{R298}{R299}.

evidence.name: Aeolus
evidence.instrument: ALADIN 355 nm direct-detection Doppler wind lidar (Rayleigh + Mie channels)
evidence.detail: First space-based Doppler wind lidar; line-of-sight wind profiles assimilated operationally at ECMWF with positive forecast impact; mission concluded 28 Jul 2023.

evidence.name: Aeolus
evidence.instrument: ALADIN Doppler wind lidar (355 nm, Rayleigh and Mie channels)
evidence.detail: First spaceborne Doppler wind lidar; winds assimilated operationally at ECMWF with positive forecast impact; laser energy below target (60 vs 80 mJ) and signal loss were documented early in the mission; mission ended 28 July 2023.

techniques.name: IPDA / DIAL greenhouse-gas lidar
techniques.summary: On/off-line pulse pairs give column CO2 or CH4 day, night and at high latitude where passive SWIR fails.
techniques.trlNote: CO2 IPDA: ACDL on DQ-1 (launched 2022-04-16){R303} has produced global XCO2 since 2022{R304}, validated against TCCON at about 0.2 ppm bias and 1.5 ppm RMSE in 2025–26 literature{R303}; TRL 9 for CO2 as of 2026-10. CH4 IPDA at 1645 nm remains unflown; MERLIN launch is listed by CNES for 2029{R305}{R306}.

evidence.name: DQ-1 (AEMS)
evidence.operator: CNSA / Ministry of Ecology and Environment, China
evidence.detail: First spaceborne IPDA lidar; global column-averaged CO2 from June 2022 onward, day and night.

evidence.name: DQ-1 (Atmospheric Environment Monitoring Satellite)
evidence.instrument: ACDL (Aerosol and Carbon dioxide Detection Lidar), 1.57 µm CO2 IPDA
evidence.detail: Global XCO2 columns from spaceborne IPDA lidar since 2022; daytime products agree with TCCON at 0.21 ppm mean bias and 1.49 ppm RMSE (R=0.92).

techniques.name: Satellite and lunar laser ranging
techniques.summary: Ground stations range to retroreflectors at mm precision; defines the terrestrial reference frame origin and tests gravity.

evidence.name: ILRS global network
evidence.instrument: Ground SLR/LLR stations ranging to retroreflector satellites and lunar arrays
evidence.detail: Operational service producing mm-level ranges; defines the ITRF origin and scale contribution.

evidence.name: LAGEOS-1 / LAGEOS-2
evidence.detail: Primary SLR geodetic targets for geocenter, Earth rotation and gravity (GM, J2) studies.

evidence.name: Apollo / Lunokhod lunar retroreflectors
evidence.instrument: Apollo 11/14/15 and Lunokhod 1/2 arrays ranged by LLR stations (APOLLO, OCA)
evidence.detail: Millimetre-level lunar laser ranging tests of gravity (equivalence principle, G-dot) continuing for five decades.

techniques.name: Inter-satellite microwave and laser ranging
techniques.summary: Range-rate between two co-orbiting spacecraft at nm/s maps time-variable gravity: groundwater, ice mass, ocean bottom pressure.

evidence.name: GRACE
evidence.instrument: K/Ka-band microwave ranging (KBR) between twin satellites
evidence.detail: Monthly time-variable gravity fields; groundwater, ice mass and ocean bottom pressure.

evidence.name: GRACE-FO
evidence.instrument: KBR plus Laser Ranging Interferometer (LRI, 1064 nm)
evidence.detail: Continues the mass-change record; LRI demonstrated nm/sqrt(Hz) range noise in orbit, first inter-satellite laser interferometer.

techniques.name: Electrostatic gravity gradiometry
techniques.summary: Six accelerometers on a rigid frame measure second derivatives of the geopotential; static geoid to 1–2 cm at 100 km.

evidence.name: GOCE
evidence.instrument: EGG three-axis electrostatic gravity gradiometer (six accelerometers) with GPS
evidence.detail: Static geoid to 1–2 cm and gravity anomalies to 1 mGal at ~100 km resolution.

techniques.name: Gravity from precise orbit determination
techniques.examples: CHAMP, Swarm, LAGEOS, every geodetic satellite
techniques.summary: Orbit perturbations invert to the gravity field; the oldest space-geodetic observable (Vanguard's pear-shaped Earth, 1958).

evidence.name: Vanguard 1
evidence.instrument: Optical/radio tracking of satellite orbit perturbations
evidence.detail: Orbit analysis revealed the J3 'pear-shaped' zonal harmonic; origin of satellite gravimetry.

evidence.name: CHAMP
evidence.instrument: GPS high-low satellite-to-satellite tracking plus STAR accelerometer
evidence.detail: EIGEN-1S and successors: first high-quality global gravity fields from GPS tracking of a LEO satellite.

evidence.name: Swarm
evidence.instrument: GPS receivers on three satellites used for gravity recovery
evidence.detail: Multi-approach Swarm GPS gravity field models bridge the GRACE/GRACE-FO gap.

evidence.name: LAGEOS-1/2
evidence.instrument: SLR tracking of passive geodetic spheres
evidence.detail: Long-wavelength gravity field and its temporal variations from precise orbit determination.

techniques.name: Vector and scalar magnetometry
techniques.summary: Fluxgate plus absolute scalar (Overhauser or He-4) instruments map the core, crustal and ionospheric fields; Swarm's He-4 magnetometer is a flown quantum sensor.

evidence.name: MAGSAT
evidence.instrument: Fluxgate vector magnetometer plus cesium-vapor scalar magnetometer
evidence.detail: First global vector survey of the geomagnetic field from orbit.

evidence.name: Ørsted
evidence.instrument: Compact Spherical Coil fluxgate plus Overhauser proton scalar magnetometer
evidence.detail: High-precision vector and scalar field data for the IGRF and core-field models.

evidence.name: CHAMP
evidence.instrument: Fluxgate vector magnetometers plus Overhauser scalar magnetometer
evidence.detail: Decade-long magnetic field survey underpinning crustal and core-field models.

evidence.name: Swarm
evidence.instrument: VFM fluxgate plus ASM helium-4 optically pumped absolute scalar magnetometer (three satellites)
evidence.detail: Operational constellation; the ASM is a flown quantum (optically pumped He-4) sensor with in-orbit results reported 2016.

techniques.name: Electric field and plasma instruments
techniques.examples: Swarm EFI, DMSP SSIES, C/NOFS, MMS
techniques.summary: Langmuir probes, ion drift meters and double probes sample the plasma the spacecraft flies through; in-situ but treated as remote sensing of the ionosphere.

evidence.name: Swarm
evidence.instrument: EFI: thermal ion imagers and Langmuir probes
evidence.detail: Ion drift, density and temperature along three LEO orbits.

evidence.name: DMSP
evidence.instrument: SSIES ion drift meter, retarding potential analyzer, Langmuir probe
evidence.detail: Routine ionospheric plasma drift and convection monitoring on the DMSP series.

evidence.name: C/NOFS
evidence.instrument: Ion velocity meter, planar Langmuir probe, vector electric field instrument
evidence.detail: Equatorial ionospheric plasma and electric-field measurements for scintillation forecasting.

evidence.name: MMS
evidence.instrument: FIELDS double-probe electric field instruments plus plasma analyzers (four spacecraft)
evidence.detail: In-situ electric field and plasma measurements in the magnetosphere.

techniques.name: Energetic particle detectors and cutoff rigidity
techniques.examples: GOES SEISS, Van Allen Probes, PAMELA, AMS-02
techniques.summary: Geomagnetic cutoff of cosmic-ray arrival directions maps the field's shielding; radiation-belt dynamics from particle spectra.

evidence.name: GOES-R series (GOES-16/17/18/19)
evidence.instrument: SEISS: MPS-LO/HI, SGPS, EHIS energetic particle sensors
evidence.detail: Operational radiation-belt and solar energetic particle monitoring from GEO.

evidence.name: Van Allen Probes (RBSP)
evidence.instrument: ECT, RBSPICE, REPT, EMFISIS particle and field suites
evidence.detail: Radiation-belt dynamics from twin-spacecraft particle spectra.

evidence.name: Resurs-DK1 / PAMELA
evidence.instrument: Magnetic spectrometer for cosmic-ray antimatter and nuclei
evidence.detail: Cosmic-ray spectra and geomagnetic cutoff studies from a polar LEO.

evidence.name: ISS / AMS-02
evidence.instrument: Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, GeV–TeV cosmic rays
evidence.detail: Precision cosmic-ray fluxes; rigidity-dependent geomagnetic cutoff exploited in the analysis.

techniques.name: Planetary gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy
techniques.examples: Lunar Prospector, Mars Odyssey GRS/HEND, MESSENGER, LRO LEND, Dawn GRaND
techniques.summary: Galactic cosmic rays excite nuclei in the top meter of regolith; leaked gamma lines and neutron albedo give elemental abundance and hydrogen. Earth's atmosphere is too thick for this from orbit.

evidence.name: Lunar Prospector
evidence.detail: Global lunar elemental maps and polar hydrogen (epithermal neutron deficit).

evidence.name: Mars Odyssey
evidence.instrument: GRS suite: gamma-ray spectrometer, HEND and neutron spectrometer
evidence.detail: Global Mars elemental abundance and near-surface hydrogen maps.

evidence.name: MESSENGER
evidence.detail: Mercury surface composition from orbit 2011–2015.

evidence.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
evidence.detail: Lunar polar hydrogen mapping with collimated epithermal neutrons.

techniques.name: Cosmic-ray air-shower fluorescence from orbit
techniques.summary: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays make N2 fluoresce along the shower; the same fast UV cameras see transient luminous events and meteors.
techniques.trlNote: Mini-EUSO (ISS, 2019–) and TUS operated in orbit and observed TLEs and meteors{R345}{R346}{R347}; after five years Mini-EUSO reports no confirmed UHECR detection (ICRC 2025 proceedings, 2026){R347}. No orbital successor is scheduled; the POEMMA balloon flies 2027{R348}. TRL 6 as of 2026-10.

evidence.name: Mini-EUSO
evidence.instrument: Fresnel-lens UV telescope with 36 MAPMTs, 2.5 us frames, 300–400 nm
evidence.detail: Operating on the ISS since Aug 2019 looking nadir through a UV-transparent window; measures UV night emissions, TLEs and meteors and validates the detector chain for UHECR fluorescence; no UHECR shower detection claimed from orbit yet.

evidence.name: TUS (Lomonosov)
evidence.detail: First orbital UHECR fluorescence detector; recorded candidate extensive air shower events and many TLE/anthropogenic flashes before satellite failure.

evidence.name: POEMMA
evidence.detail: Mission concept for UHECR fluorescence and neutrino Cherenkov detection from orbit.

evidence.name: Mini-EUSO
evidence.instrument: UV (300–400 nm) Fresnel-lens telescope with 2304-pixel MAPMT focal surface on the ISS Zvezda nadir window
evidence.detail: Operating on the ISS since 7 Oct 2019 (~750 h of data over 5 years); detected >22,000 meteors and 37 elves; no UHECR events, instrument capable of placing an upper limit above 1e21 eV.

evidence.name: TUS on Lomonosov
evidence.instrument: UV fluorescence telescope (2 m² mirror, 256-pixel PMT camera)
evidence.detail: First orbital UHECR fluorescence detector; registered TLEs, meteors and candidate EAS-like events.

evidence.name: POEMMA-Balloon with Radio (PBR)
evidence.instrument: 1.1 m Schmidt telescope with fluorescence and Cherenkov cameras plus radio antennas
evidence.operator: NASA super-pressure balloon programme / POEMMA collaboration
evidence.detail: Pathfinder balloon flight from Wanaka, NZ, planned for 2027; no orbital successor scheduled.

techniques.name: Stellar occultation
techniques.examples: GOMOS (Envisat), UVS instruments at planets, New Horizons
techniques.summary: Star setting behind the limb gives ozone, NO2 and density profiles; hundreds of stars nightly, self-calibrating.

evidence.name: Envisat
evidence.detail: Hundreds of stellar occultations per night; ozone, NO2, NO3, aerosol and density profiles; self-calibrating ratio to the unocculted star.

evidence.name: Cassini
evidence.instrument: UVIS ultraviolet imaging spectrograph with HSP occultation channel
evidence.detail: Stellar occultations of Saturn's atmosphere and rings; representative of planetary UVS occultation instruments.

evidence.name: New Horizons
evidence.instrument: Alice UV imaging spectrograph with solar occultation channel
evidence.detail: UV spectrograph designed for solar and stellar occultations; probed Pluto's atmosphere during the 2015 flyby.

techniques.name: Geodetic VLBI
techniques.summary: Cross-correlating quasar signals at ground stations measures baselines to mm and Earth orientation; the only flown correlation receiver using a cosmic source. Space-VLBI (RadioAstron) extended the baseline.

evidence.name: IVS global network
evidence.instrument: S/X-band legacy geodetic VLBI antennas and correlators
evidence.operator: International VLBI Service for Geodesy and Astrometry
evidence.detail: Operational service for Earth orientation (UT1, nutation), the celestial frame and station coordinates.

evidence.name: VGOS
evidence.detail: Broadband VLBI demonstrated mm-level baseline precision; operational VGOS sessions since 2017–2019.

evidence.name: RadioAstron (Spektr-R)
evidence.instrument: 10 m space radio telescope forming space–ground VLBI baselines to ~350,000 km
evidence.detail: Space-VLBI extended the baseline beyond Earth's diameter.

techniques.name: Pulsar-timing navigation
techniques.summary: Millisecond pulsar arrival times fix spacecraft position to ~km; positioning rather than Earth sensing, but it fills the cosmic × time-of-flight cell.
techniques.trlNote: SEXTANT demonstrated X-ray pulsar navigation on the ISS in November 2017 (position within 10 km in about 8 h){R359}{R360}{R361}.

evidence.name: NICER / SEXTANT (ISS)
evidence.instrument: NICER X-ray timing instrument used by the SEXTANT navigation experiment
evidence.detail: On-orbit demonstration of autonomous X-ray pulsar navigation: millisecond-pulsar arrival times gave ISS position to <10 km within hours. Remaining for TRL 9: a dedicated flight navigation system used operationally.

evidence.name: SEXTANT on NICER (ISS)
evidence.instrument: NICER X-ray Timing Instrument (56 concentrator optics / SDDs) with SEXTANT flight software
evidence.detail: Autonomous real-time X-ray pulsar navigation demonstrated on the ISS starting 9 Nov 2017: <10 km RSS orbit error within ~7.5 h over a 2.2-day run; additional on-orbit results reported 2018. Remaining before TRL 9: operation on a free-flying spacecraft as the primary navigation source.

techniques.name: GNSS radio occultation
techniques.examples: COSMIC-2, Metop GRAS, Spire, PlanetiQ, GeoOptics
techniques.summary: Bending angle of GNSS rays through the limb inverts to refractivity, then temperature and moisture at ~100 m vertical resolution, bias-free.

evidence.name: COSMIC-2 / FORMOSAT-7
evidence.instrument: TGRS GNSS radio occultation receivers on six satellites
evidence.detail: Operational tropical RO constellation; >4000 profiles/day assimilated by NWP centres.

evidence.name: Metop GRAS
evidence.instrument: GNSS Receiver for Atmospheric Sounding on Metop-A/B/C
evidence.detail: Operational RO profiles assimilated in NWP since 2007.

evidence.name: Spire Lemur constellation
evidence.detail: Commercial RO data assessed and purchased by NOAA/EUMETSAT.

evidence.name: PlanetiQ GNOMES
evidence.detail: Commercial RO constellation; refractivity validated against ERA5.

techniques.name: GNSS reflectometry
techniques.summary: Delay-Doppler maps of forward-scattered GNSS signals give ocean wind, soil moisture, flooding, sea ice; a bistatic radar with free transmitters.

evidence.name: TechDemoSat-1
evidence.detail: First systematic spaceborne GNSS-R delay-Doppler maps; ocean wind speed retrievals.

evidence.name: CYGNSS
evidence.instrument: Eight microsatellites with DDMI GNSS-R receivers
evidence.detail: Operational science mission for ocean winds in tropical cyclones; also soil moisture and inundation products.

evidence.name: Spire Lemur constellation
evidence.detail: Coherent grazing-angle reflections for altimetry and sea ice.

evidence.name: FY-3E
evidence.instrument: GNOS-II GNSS occultation and reflectometry receiver
evidence.detail: Operational meteorological satellite carrying GNSS-R; first results for wind and soil moisture.

techniques.name: Polarimetric GNSS-R
techniques.examples: Airborne campaigns, SMAP radar-receiver reuse studies
techniques.summary: Polarization ratio of the reflected signal separates dielectric from roughness effects for soil moisture and vegetation.
techniques.trlNote: Airborne campaigns only{R376}.

evidence.name: Airborne polarimetric GNSS-R (GRASS campaigns)
evidence.detail: Polarimetric ratio of reflected GNSS signals correlated with soil moisture and above-ground biomass over agricultural and forest sites in Italy.

evidence.name: SMAP radar receiver reflectometry (SMAP-R)
evidence.instrument: SMAP L-band radar receiver repurposed to record GPS reflections in H and V polarization
evidence.detail: Opportunistic spaceborne polarimetric GNSS-R assessment over land and cryosphere after the SMAP radar transmitter failed.

evidence.name: Airborne polarimetric GNSS-R (GRASS receiver) campaigns
evidence.detail: Polarimetric ratio of GNSS reflections related to soil moisture and above-ground biomass over agricultural and forest sites.

evidence.name: SMAP radar receiver reuse (SMAP-Reflectometry)
evidence.instrument: SMAP L-band radar receiver (H and V) recording GPS L2C reflections
evidence.detail: Opportunistic spaceborne polarimetric GNSS-R scatterometry over land and cryosphere assessed from SMAP's radar receiver after the radar transmitter failure.

techniques.name: GNSS-R altimetry and snow/ice sensing
techniques.examples: TDS-1 altimetry and sea-ice detection, ground GNSS-IR snow depth
techniques.summary: Delay of the specular point gives dm-level surface height; L-band penetrates dry snow so the reflection encodes depth.
techniques.trlNote: TDS-1 altimetry demonstrated in orbit at research grade{R378}; ground GNSS-IR snow depth is operational{R379}{R380}.

evidence.name: TechDemoSat-1 GNSS-R altimetry
evidence.detail: First spaceborne GNSS-R sea-surface height, ~8 m precision from code-delay tracking; sea-ice detection also demonstrated.

evidence.name: CYGNSS sea-ice sensing
evidence.detail: Sea-ice extent/type classification from CYGNSS and TDS-1 DDMs reviewed; research products.

evidence.name: Ground GNSS-IR snow depth
evidence.instrument: Geodetic GPS receivers (PBO network) using SNR multipath
evidence.detail: Snow depth retrieved from GPS signal-to-noise interference patterns at continuously operating stations.

evidence.name: TechDemoSat-1
evidence.detail: First spaceborne GNSS-R sea-surface height observations (research grade, several-metre precision) and sea-ice detection from TDS-1 DDMs.

evidence.name: Ground GNSS interferometric reflectometry (PBO H2O network)
evidence.detail: Snow depth from GPS-IR demonstrated and run as a routine product across western US geodetic sites.

techniques.name: Ionospheric TEC from dual-frequency GNSS
techniques.summary: Dispersive delay between frequencies is proportional to electron content along the path; the backbone of ionospheric monitoring.

evidence.name: IGS global GNSS network (ground)
evidence.instrument: Dual-frequency GNSS receivers, IGS ionosphere working group
evidence.detail: Global VTEC maps produced routinely since 1998 from dual-frequency slant TEC.

evidence.name: COSMIC-2 / FORMOSAT-7
evidence.detail: Electron-density profiles and TEC from LEO dual-frequency tracking.

evidence.name: Swarm
evidence.instrument: Dual-frequency GPS receivers on three satellites
evidence.detail: Topside TEC along the orbit derived from the precise orbit determination GPS receivers.

techniques.name: Passive bistatic radar with broadcast illuminators
techniques.examples: Ground and airborne demos; passive SAR with Starlink downlinks in the literature
techniques.summary: Correlate a reference channel against surface echoes of a comm or broadcast signal to image or track with no transmitter of your own.
techniques.trlNote: Ground and airborne demonstrations only, including Starlink-illuminated passive SAR imagery (IEEE JSTARS 2024){R385} and a German MoD Starlink passive radar (2024-01); no orbital receiver has flown and none is on a near-term manifest. TRL 5 as of 2026-10.

evidence.name: DVB-T passive SAR demonstrator
evidence.instrument: Ground/airborne passive radar correlating DVB-T reference and surveillance channels
evidence.detail: Passive SAR images formed from DVB-T illuminators of opportunity.

evidence.name: Starlink-based passive radar
evidence.instrument: Ku-band passive radar demonstrator using Starlink user-downlink as illuminator
evidence.detail: First passive SAR images of Earth's surface under Starlink illumination (direct and adjacent-cell).

evidence.name: Starlink-illuminated passive SAR demonstrator
evidence.instrument: Dual-channel Ku-band passive radar receiver (Starlink user downlink as illuminator), back-projection imaging
evidence.detail: First passive SAR images of urban areas formed from Starlink downlink echoes with a ground-based receiver.

techniques.name: Free-space optical link scintillometry
techniques.summary: Intensity fluctuations on satellite–ground laser links measure integrated turbulence and extinction; characterized per link, not yet used as a sensing network.
techniques.trlNote: Characterized on OICETS{R388}, LCRD{R389}{R390} and EDRS{R391} links; not yet used as a sensing product.

evidence.name: OICETS (Kirari) KODEN link campaign
evidence.instrument: LUCE laser terminal to NICT optical ground station
evidence.detail: LEO–ground laser links with scintillation index and coherence-length statistics measured on the link.

evidence.name: ARTEMIS GEO–ground laser link statistics
evidence.instrument: SILEX terminal to ESA OGS Tenerife
evidence.detail: Long-term statistics of laser beam propagation (scintillation, fade) on a GEO–ground link.

evidence.name: LCRD downlink turbulence profiling
evidence.instrument: LCRD GEO 1550 nm downlink observed with RINGSS profiler at Table Mountain
evidence.detail: Vertical optical turbulence profiles measured from the satellite laser beam, correlated with other monitors (R=0.75–0.86).

evidence.name: OICETS (Kirari) – NICT optical ground station (KODEN)
evidence.instrument: LUCE laser terminal on OICETS; 1.5 m NICT OGS
evidence.detail: Downlink scintillation index on LEO–ground laser links measured and found consistent with strong-fluctuation theory; uplink multi-beam scintillation reduction characterized.

evidence.name: LCRD – JPL Optical Ground Station 1 (Table Mountain)
evidence.instrument: LCRD GEO laser terminals; OGS-1 with Atmospheric Channel Monitoring system and adaptive optics
evidence.detail: GEO–ground optical link and atmospheric turbulence characterized per link at OGS-1 during the LCRD experiment phase; not used as a sensing product.

techniques.name: Interferometric aperture-synthesis radiometry from GEO
techniques.summary: A sparse array correlated in real time synthesizes a filled aperture for microwave sounding from GEO, where a mechanical dish would be impractically large.
techniques.trlNote: GeoSTAR and GIMS/GIMS-II are ground demonstrators{R395}{R396}{R397}. China's FY-4M geostationary microwave sounder is planned for launch from late 2026 with more than 100 channels (WMO OSCAR; AMT 2026); no authoritative source describes its antenna architecture, so whether it is aperture synthesis or a real aperture is unconfirmed{R398}{R399}. TRL 5 as of 2026-10; re-check at FY-4M launch.

evidence.name: GeoSTAR demonstrator
evidence.instrument: Y-shaped 24-element 50–56 GHz synthetic thinned array radiometer
evidence.detail: Ground demonstrator produced synthesized brightness-temperature images at 50 GHz, validating the GEO sounder concept.

evidence.name: GIMS demonstrator
evidence.instrument: Rotating thinned-array interferometric microwave sounder at 50–56 GHz
evidence.detail: Ground-based imaging demonstrator; first interferometric images and analysis supporting a GEO sounder.

evidence.name: GeoSTAR demonstrator
evidence.detail: Ground demonstrator produced interferometric brightness-temperature images at 50–56 GHz; validated the aperture-synthesis concept for GEO sounding.

evidence.name: GIMS / GIMS-II demonstrators
evidence.instrument: Rotating thinned-array interferometric radiometer at 50–56 GHz (GIMS) and 183 GHz (GIMS-II)
evidence.detail: Imaging demonstrations with the GIMS rotating-array prototype and preliminary GIMS-II results reported; ground only.

evidence.name: FY-4M1
evidence.instrument: MWS (Microwave Sounder for Geostationary Orbit), >100 channels
evidence.detail: Listed in WMO OSCAR as planned (launch ≥2026); 2026 AMT paper states launch planned for end of 2026; antenna architecture not described in available primary sources.

techniques.name: Cold-atom accelerometry demonstration
techniques.summary: Atom-interferometer accelerometers have operated in microgravity; the step to a gradiometer is the concept in the next list.
techniques.trlNote: Atom-interferometer inertial sensing has been demonstrated in orbit: NASA CAL dual-species interferometry (ISS, Nature 2023){R400}{R401}{R402} and CSSAI on Tiangong (cold-atom gyroscope and accelerometer, about 1 µm s⁻² and 17 µrad s⁻¹, 2024–25){R327}. Gravimetry-grade performance has not been shown; the CARIOQA pathfinder has its engineering model in fabrication for a launch by the end of the decade (DLR){R403}. TRL 7 as of 2026-10.

evidence.name: NASA Cold Atom Lab (ISS)
evidence.instrument: Rb/K BEC apparatus with atom-interferometer capability
evidence.detail: BECs produced in orbit (2020) and pathfinder atom-interferometer measurements in microgravity (2024); not yet a sensor-grade accelerometer.

evidence.name: China Space Station Atom Interferometer (CSSAI)
evidence.instrument: Dual-species Rb atom interferometer in the High Microgravity rack
evidence.operator: CAS Innovation Academy for Precision Measurement / CMSA
evidence.detail: Cold-atom gyroscope/accelerometer operated in orbit: rotation resolution ~17 urad/s and acceleration ~1 um/s^2, cross-checked against the station gyroscopes. Remaining: gradiometer configuration and sensor-grade performance.

evidence.name: CARIOQA-PMP
evidence.instrument: Rb cold-atom quantum accelerometer engineering model for a pathfinder mission
evidence.detail: Pathfinder mission preparation only; engineering model under development, not yet flown.

evidence.name: Cold Atom Lab (ISS)
evidence.detail: Launched 21 May 2018; first dual-species atom interferometry and pathfinder inertial-sensing/photon-recoil measurements in orbit; sensitivity limited by ISS vibrations; gravimetry-grade performance not shown.

evidence.name: China Space Station Atom Interferometer (CSSAI)
evidence.detail: Launched to the CSS Nov 2022; rotation resolution 50 µrad/s single shot (17 µrad/s averaged over 32) and acceleration resolution 1.0 µm/s² single shot reported in 2025. Remaining before TRL 9: gradiometer configuration and gravimetry-grade performance (CARIOQA pathfinder in preparation).

techniques.name: Hosted star-tracker exploitation
techniques.examples: Space-domain awareness from commercial star trackers
techniques.summary: Sunlit debris and satellites streak through star-tracker fields; existing hardware repurposed for orbit determination.
techniques.trlNote: On-orbit star-tracker data exploited for SDA{R406}{R407}.

evidence.name: Star-tracker-like on-orbit imagery for RSO detection
evidence.instrument: Fast Auroral Imager (e-POP/Swarm-Echo) imagery used as star-tracker analogue
evidence.detail: Detection and tracking of faint resident space objects demonstrated on real on-orbit low-resolution imagery (878 images, 2191 RSOs; 79% precision, 71% recall). Remaining: demonstration on an actual hosted commercial star tracker with orbit-determination products.

evidence.name: Dual-use star tracker / SDA sensor in-space test
evidence.instrument: Commercial star tracker imagery processed for resident-space-object detection
evidence.detail: In-space test of a dual-use star tracker as a space-domain-awareness sensor reported at AMOS 2021; RSOnet framework shows star trackers are a feasible LEO RSO detection source using real in-space detections. Remaining before TRL 9: routine orbit-determination product from hosted star trackers.

techniques.name: Raman lidar (ground and airborne)
techniques.examples: Ground Raman lidars, airborne water-vapor Raman
techniques.summary: Vibrational Raman return gives water vapor and temperature without assumptions; from orbit the photon budget is roughly 10³× short.
techniques.trlNote: Ground Raman lidar is TRL 9{R409}. From orbit the photon budget fails by ~10³; studies only{R410}.

evidence.name: NASA GSFC Raman lidar
evidence.instrument: Nd:YAG 355 nm Raman lidar, N2 and H2O channels
evidence.detail: Water-vapor mixing ratio and aerosol profiles from vibrational Raman return; established ground technique.

evidence.name: RASL airborne Raman lidar
evidence.instrument: Raman Airborne Spectroscopic Lidar on NASA aircraft
evidence.detail: Airborne water-vapor and temperature Raman profiling; photon budget scaled to orbit is roughly three orders of magnitude short.

evidence.name: Ground-based Raman lidar (NASA GSFC Scanning Raman Lidar lineage)
evidence.instrument: Nd:YAG/XeF Raman lidar for water vapor and aerosols
evidence.detail: Vibrational Raman water-vapor and aerosol profiling established from the ground (TRL 9 on the ground).

evidence.name: Spaceborne Raman lidar concept
evidence.instrument: Simulated space-borne Raman lidar for temperature/water vapor
evidence.operator: University of Basilicata / University of Hohenheim
evidence.detail: Performance simulations show space-borne Raman profiling requires very large power-aperture products; studies only.

techniques.name: Laser-induced fluorescence lidar (ocean, vegetation)
techniques.summary: Pulse-excited fluorescence of chlorophyll, CDOM and oil gives composition the elastic return cannot.
techniques.trlNote: Airborne oceanographic and oil-spill fluorosensors{R412}{R413}.

evidence.name: NASA Airborne Oceanographic Lidar (AOL)
evidence.instrument: Pulsed 532 nm laser with spectrometer for Raman and fluorescence
evidence.detail: Simultaneous water Raman, chlorophyll-a fluorescence and oil-film thickness measurement from aircraft.

evidence.name: Oil-spill laser fluorosensors (airborne)
evidence.detail: Operational airborne fluorosensors discriminate oil type and CDOM; reviewed in oceanographic lidar literature.

evidence.name: NASA Airborne Oceanographic Lidar (AOL)
evidence.instrument: Laser fluorosensor (water Raman and chlorophyll-a fluorescence)
evidence.detail: Airborne simultaneous detection of laser-induced water Raman backscatter and chlorophyll/pigment fluorescence.

evidence.name: Airborne oil-spill laser fluorosensors (e.g., LEAF/SLEAF)
evidence.detail: Review of airborne laser fluorosensor development and operational trials for oil-spill detection and classification.

concepts.name: Rydberg-atom RF electrometry from orbit
concepts.physics: Atoms excited to Rydberg states have enormous electric dipole moments. An RF field resonant with a Rydberg transition splits the electromagnetically-induced-transparency line by the Rabi frequency, which is set by the field amplitude and a known dipole matrix element. The readout is therefore self-calibrated to SI units, tunable from ~MHz to THz, and needs no wavelength-sized antenna.
concepts.application: Broadband passive microwave radiometry and RF geolocation in a CubeSat volume; THz limb sounding without heterodyne front-ends.
concepts.failure: Sensitivity still trails cryogenic LNAs by an order of magnitude or more; laser and vapor-cell reliability in vacuum and radiation. The win is bandwidth and calibration, not noise floor.
concepts.first: Compare noise-equivalent field against a state-of-the-art radiometer at 6, 37 and 183 GHz for the same integration time.
concepts.prior: Spaceborne Rydberg-atom RF sensing is the target of funded agency programs: NASA NIAC Phase I/II Quantum Rydberg Radar (JPL, 2023; balloon demonstration planned){R416}, NASA ESTO's QuARREM Rydberg hyperspectral radiometer (ColdQuanta, now Infleqtion, selected under ACT-22 in December 2022){R417}, ground soil-moisture reflectometry with satellite signals of opportunity (Arumugam et al., Sci. Rep. 2024){R418}. No on-orbit flight reported. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Lab and field demos of Rydberg receivers{R419}{R418}; no space-environment validation.

evidence.name: Quantum Rydberg Radar (NIAC Phase I) satellite-signal reception
evidence.detail: Phase I reported the first known Rydberg-atom measurement of satellite (XM) signals from the ground; Phase II (2023) prepares a high-altitude balloon demonstration. Not yet flown.

evidence.name: Rydberg soil-moisture reflectometry with satellite signals of opportunity
evidence.detail: Ground-based radar reflectometry: atoms sensitised to XM satellite radio signals; signal correlations used to retrieve soil moisture.

evidence.name: QuARREM Rydberg vapour-cell radiometer front-end
evidence.instrument: atomic vapour-cell hyperspectral microwave radiometer (20–200 GHz)
evidence.operator: ColdQuanta/Infleqtion with Ball Aerospace, NASA ESTO ACT-22
evidence.detail: ACT-22 task set: modelling, testbench, vapour-cell fabrication, absolute calibration; measurement chamber to advance TRL 2 to 4.

evidence.name: Rydberg EIT vapour-cell microwave electrometry
evidence.instrument: Rb/Cs vapour cell, EIT Autler-Townes readout
evidence.operator: University of Oklahoma / Stuttgart (Shaffer, Pfau groups) and others
evidence.detail: SI-traceable field amplitude from Autler-Townes splitting demonstrated in 2012; many laboratory receiver demonstrations reviewed by 2021.

evidence.name: Quantum Rydberg Radar balloon demonstration
evidence.detail: NIAC Phase II targets a high-altitude balloon demonstration and a future space validation; no flight reported.

concepts.name: Orbital laser Doppler vibrometry
concepts.physics: A heterodyne lidar resolves surface velocity via Δf = 2v/λ; at 1.5 µm, 1 mm/s is 1.3 kHz. Machinery, engines and structures vibrate at characteristic frequencies that show up as sidebands on the return.
concepts.application: Industrial activity monitoring, centrifuge-hall and generator signatures, bridge and dam modal health.
concepts.failure: Platform velocity of 7.5 km/s and speckle decorrelation limit coherent integration to microseconds. Needs a co-located reference return (a static surface or retroreflector) for differential measurement, and dwell long enough to resolve the vibration lines.
concepts.first: Speckle decorrelation time vs spot size and orbital velocity, then the achievable frequency resolution per dwell.
concepts.prior: Proposed by JPL as an orbital vibrometer for ground targets (NASA Tech Briefs, 2009){R422} and claimed as a space use in a Caltech/NASA patent (US 8,210,044, 2012){R423}; orbital vibrometry was proposed for asteroid seismology by Sava and Asphaug (Adv. Space Res. 2019) and its speckle-noise problem analysed by Courville and Sava (Acta Astronautica 2020){R424}{R425}. Airborne and vehicle LDV are demonstrated; no orbital demonstration against Earth targets found. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Airborne LDV validates the sensor, not the orbital speckle-decorrelation problem.

evidence.name: Orbital covert laser vibrometry concept (JPL)
evidence.instrument: narrow-band laser illuminator with lock-in receiver and whispering-gallery-mode filter
evidence.detail: Tech Brief and patent describe a system placed in Earth orbit measuring ground-object vibrations at ranges of thousands of km; concept and patent claims only, no hardware demonstration reported.

evidence.name: Orbital laser Doppler vibrometer seismology (small bodies)
evidence.operator: Colorado School of Mines / University of Arizona
evidence.detail: Concept and speckle-noise analysis for an orbiting LDV reading surface seismic motion of asteroids; speckle decorrelation identified and mitigation strategies simulated.

concepts.name: Space-to-sodium-layer magnetometry
concepts.physics: Sodium atoms at 85–95 km, excited by a 589 nm laser, precess in the geomagnetic field at the Larmor frequency. Modulating the laser at that frequency drives spin polarization and changes fluorescence; sweeping the modulation finds the resonance and hence |B| to nT.
concepts.application: Global mesospheric magnetometry along track; a layer no in-situ instrument occupies, sensitive to ionospheric current systems.
concepts.failure: Laser power and beam quality from orbit; fluorescence photon budget at 500+ km; competing OH and background light. Ground systems already do this with 20 W lasers over ~90 km paths.
concepts.first: Fluorescence photon rate at the spacecraft for a 20 W CW laser and a 1 m aperture; compare to shot-noise requirement for 1 nT.
concepts.prior: Ground sodium-layer magnetometry was proposed by Higbie et al. (PNAS 2011){R426} and demonstrated by Kane et al. (JGR 2018){R427}. A satellite-assisted variant with the laser on the ground and a polarimeter in LEO was proposed by Dang et al. (2021; Optics Continuum 2022){R428}. The all-from-orbit configuration with the laser on the spacecraft has not been proposed in detail or flown. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground LGS magnetometry proves the physics{R427}{R429}; space geometry untested.

evidence.name: Ground laser remote magnetometry of mesospheric sodium
evidence.instrument: 589 nm modulated laser guide star + fluorescence photometry
evidence.operator: Kane et al. (US) and Pedreros Bustos et al. (ESO/Mainz, La Palma)
evidence.detail: Larmor-resonance detection in sodium-layer fluorescence from the ground; mesospheric geomagnetic field magnitude measured at 85–95 km.

evidence.name: Sodium-layer magnetometry proposal
evidence.detail: Theory and sensitivity estimates for measuring the mesospheric field with a modulated sodium laser.

evidence.name: Satellite-assisted sodium magnetometry (ground laser, LEO polarimeter)
evidence.detail: Proposal and modelling of a LEO polarimetric detector observing ground-laser-pumped sodium; not flown.

concepts.name: Powerline flicker sensing from orbit
concepts.physics: LED and discharge lamps modulate at twice the mains frequency (100 or 120 Hz) with modulation depth of a few to tens of percent. A photon-counting array sampled above 300 Hz on a small nighttime field of view recovers the modulation frequency and phase.
concepts.application: Map which regions run on which synchronous grid; detect islanding, generator-powered sites, and frequency excursions that precede grid stress; identify off-grid installations.
concepts.failure: Photon rate is not the limit (see TRL basis). The risks are platform: holding a 100 m cell for a second from LEO needs body pointing or back-scan, pointing-jitter power near 100–120 Hz masquerades as signal, and mixed lamp types can dilute the modulation depth below 1 %.
concepts.first: Photon rate for a 100 m ground pixel at typical urban radiance with a 30 cm aperture; SNR at 120 Hz over a 1 s dwell.
concepts.prior: Flicker-based grid sensing is established from the ground (Bianco et al., NYC hypertemporal imaging, 2016{R430}; Sheinin et al., ICCP 2018{R431}). From orbit, Elvidge et al. (Remote Sensing 2022) showed that VIIRS DNB's millisecond dwell aliases lighting flicker into nightly radiance variance without resolving frequency or phase{R432}. No spaceborne or airborne sensor sampling above Nyquist to recover mains frequency was found; the earlier airborne claim did not survive a search. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: First calculation run 2026-10-17 (scripts/calc/c04_powerline_flicker.py). A 30 cm aperture at 500 km collects about 3×10⁶ detected photons per second from a 100 m urban pixel at 100 nW cm⁻² sr⁻¹ and 3×10⁵ from a suburban one. With 10 % effective modulation the 120 Hz line has SNR of order 100 and 40 over a 1 s stare, and depths below 1 % stay detectable. Photons are not the limit; TRL 3 on the analytic budget. Untested: the 1 s stare on a 100 m cell against 7 km s⁻¹ ground motion, and pointing jitter near 100–120 Hz.

evidence.name: Ground-based flicker/phase imaging of city lighting
evidence.operator: NYU CUSP (Bianco et al.); Technion/Toronto (Sheinin et al.)
evidence.detail: Mains-frequency flicker phase of urban lights recovered from the ground (NYC hypertemporal imaging; rolling-shutter electric-grid imaging).

evidence.name: VIIRS Day/Night Band flicker aliasing analysis
evidence.operator: Payne Institute / Colorado School of Mines (Elvidge et al.) using NOAA/NASA data
evidence.detail: Analysis of on-orbit DNB data: 2–3 ms dwell aliases AC flicker into nightly radiance variance; flicker frequency and phase are not resolved. No orbital sensor sampling above Nyquist.

concepts.name: Opportunistic laser occultation via constellation crosslinks
concepts.physics: A laser crosslink between two satellites at different orbital shells or planes can graze the limb. Refractive bending, scintillation spectrum and weak-line absorption at 1550 nm encode density, temperature, turbulence and (weakly) water vapor and CO2 along the tangent path.
concepts.application: Thousands of free occultation events per day from megaconstellations at optical wavelengths, complementing GNSS-RO with higher vertical resolution.
concepts.failure: Geometry: same-plane links at ~550 km have tangent heights near 500 km, above the atmosphere. Only inter-plane and inter-shell links graze low; link acquisition may drop the link before it reaches the troposphere. Comm lasers are fixed-wavelength, so absorption is limited to whatever lines fall in-band.
concepts.first: Sweep a real constellation's crosslink topology for tangent-height distribution vs time.
concepts.prior: Observed once, incidentally: the OICETS–ARTEMIS laser link of April 2006 recorded atmospheric power fluctuations as OICETS set behind the limb (Löscher, AMT 2010){R433}. Perlot and Sofieva (ICSOS 2009) proposed adapting laser-communication terminals for occultation sounding{R434}{R435}; Liu, Kirchengast et al. (2021) simulated LEO–LEO occultation statistics{R436}; the dedicated ACCURATE laser-occultation mission was proposed to ESA in 2005 and not selected{R437}. The megaconstellation tangent-height census has not been done. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Geometry study not yet done. The 2006 incidental occultation record on a comm link shows the signal exists in space{R433}; no retrieval has been attempted from it, so the TRL is left as judged.

evidence.name: Incidental laser occultation on OICETS–ARTEMIS optical link
evidence.instrument: LUCE (OICETS) to OPALE (ARTEMIS) laser communication terminals
evidence.detail: Received-power fluctuations recorded as the LEO–GEO beam grazed the atmosphere; shows the occultation signal exists on a space link; no geophysical retrieval attempted.

evidence.name: Optical inter-satellite links for atmospheric occultation (feasibility)
evidence.detail: Coherence loss, scintillation and tracking perturbation during occultation modelled; qualification of comm terminals for occultation sounding proposed.

evidence.name: LEO–LEO occultation constellation statistics and ACCURATE concept
evidence.detail: Event counts and coverage simulated for LEO–LEO constellations (tens of thousands of events per day for 36–72 satellites); dedicated ACCURATE mission concept published, not flown.

concepts.name: Bistatic and multistatic lidar
concepts.physics: The aerosol and cloud scattering phase function varies strongly with angle and with particle size, shape and refractive index. A transmitter on one spacecraft and receivers on others sample off-axis angles that monostatic lidar cannot reach.
concepts.application: Direct microphysical retrievals of aerosol and cloud particles; ice-crystal habit; validation of the phase functions every radiative-transfer model assumes.
concepts.failure: Signal at off-axis angles is orders of magnitude weaker than backscatter; pointing and timing across free-flyers; multiple scattering contaminates at large angles.
concepts.first: Received photons per shot at 10°, 30° and 90° scattering angle for a representative aerosol layer and 1 m receiver.
concepts.prior: Concept papers only, as far as I know{R438}.

evidence.name: Multistatic aerosol–cloud lidar in space
evidence.instrument: backscatter lidar transmitter with formation-flying off-axis receivers
evidence.detail: Theoretical information-content study; one extra receiver near 170° scattering angle greatly increases aerosol/cloud retrieval information. No hardware or flight.

concepts.name: Chronometric geodesy with optical clocks
concepts.physics: General relativity: a clock's rate shifts by ΔU/c². One centimeter of height near Earth's surface is 1.1×10⁻¹⁸ in fractional frequency. Comparing an orbiting optical clock against ground clocks over optical links measures geopotential differences directly.
concepts.application: A geoid observable independent of mass-change ranging and gradiometry; unification of height systems across continents; tests of relativity.
concepts.failure: Requires 10⁻¹⁸ clock stability in orbit and a link that transfers time at the same level through the atmosphere; ACES (2025, ISS) works at 10⁻¹⁶ with microwave clocks.
concepts.first: Verify ACES results and link performance; cost the optical-clock and link upgrade.
concepts.prior: ACES launched to the ISS on 21 April 2025 (ESA) and no peer-reviewed clock-comparison result had appeared by 2026-11-04{R439}. No optical clock has operated as a clock in orbit: the strontium lattice-clock optical system on the Chinese Space Station reached in-orbit laser stabilisation and a MOT (Rev. Sci. Instrum. 96, 2025){R440}; the I-SOC Pathfinder is placed provisionally around 2030 in the community road-map (Alonso et al. 2022){R441}. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground optical-clock chronometric geodesy demonstrated{R442}{R443}. ACES (ISS, 2025) is a microwave-clock pathfinder at the 10⁻¹⁶ level{R439}, still commissioning as of mid-2026. TRL 4 stands; re-check when the first ACES redshift or time-transfer paper appears, expected 2026–2027.

evidence.name: ACES (Atomic Clock Ensemble in Space)
evidence.instrument: PHARAO caesium fountain clock and Space Hydrogen Maser with microwave link
evidence.detail: Launched 21 April 2025, installed on ISS Columbus 25 April 2025; six-month commissioning then two-year science phase planned. Microwave clocks at the 1e-16 level, validating space-ground time-transfer links; not an optical clock and no clock-comparison result verified from an acceptable source.

evidence.name: Strontium optical lattice clock optical system aboard the Chinese Space Station
evidence.instrument: 87Sr lattice clock optical system (0.11 m3, 53.6 kg)
evidence.detail: In orbit the system achieved automated multi-stage laser frequency stabilisation and a blue magneto-optical trap of 87Sr; clock operation not reported.

evidence.name: Ground chronometric geodesy with transportable optical clocks
evidence.operator: PTB / INRIM (Grotti et al.); RIKEN / Univ. Tokyo (Takamoto et al.)
evidence.detail: Height differences measured via gravitational redshift between remote optical clocks (Alps/Turin 2018; Tokyo Skytree 2020) at the 1e-18 level.

evidence.name: I-SOC Pathfinder (optical clock on ISS)
evidence.instrument: Sr lattice clock with optical/microwave links
evidence.detail: Community road-map lists I-SOC Pathfinder as a future ISS optical clock step around 2030; no ESA mission page or schedule found.

concepts.name: Single-spacecraft atom-interferometer gravity gradiometry
concepts.physics: Two cold-atom clouds separated by a baseline are interrogated with the same laser pulses; the differential phase gives the gravity gradient with no drift, since the reference is an atomic transition rather than a proof mass.
concepts.application: GOCE-class static gravity with long-term stability; sub-surface density mapping for aquifers, magma systems, voids.
concepts.failure: Sensitivity per shot is limited by atom number and interrogation time; rotation of the spacecraft couples in; the NASA and ESA pathfinders that would settle it are now 2030-class launches.
concepts.first: Check flight status of NASA QGGPf and ESA CARIOQA before doing anything else.
concepts.prior: Neither pathfinder has flown. NASA's QGGPf (Infleqtion) is scheduled to fly no earlier than 2030; the CNES/DLR-led CARIOQA-PHB consortium kicked off its Phase B in October 2025 and has published no launch date{R444}{R445}{R446}{R447}. The only orbital atom interferometer is CSSAI on the China Space Station (Li et al., National Science Review 2025){R327}, a single-sensor gyroscope and accelerometer at the µm s⁻² level, not a gradiometer. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground atom gradiometers exist{R448} and CSSAI (2025) validated cold-atom interferometry in orbit{R327}, which supports 5; no differential two-cloud gradiometer has been validated in a relevant environment, so 4 is defensible. Pathfinders slipped to 2030 and beyond, so the number will not move in this window.

evidence.name: CSSAI (China Space Station Atom Interferometer)
evidence.operator: APM / Innovation Academy for Precision Measurement, CAS
evidence.detail: First cold-atom gyroscope realised in orbit; rotation and acceleration measured with spatial fringes, piezo-mirror rotation compensation self-calibrated in orbit. Single sensor, not a differential gradiometer.

evidence.name: Ground atom-interferometer gravity gradiometer
evidence.detail: Outdoor detection of a buried tunnel by differential gravity-gradient measurement; validates the two-cloud differential configuration on the ground.

evidence.name: Quantum Gravity Gradiometer Pathfinder (QGGPf)
evidence.instrument: two-cloud ultracold Rb atom-interferometer gradiometer (~0.25 m3, ~125 kg)
evidence.operator: NASA JPL with Infleqtion, AOSense, Goddard and Vector Atomic (ESTO)
evidence.detail: Technology-validation mission to LEO; NASA states launch near the end of the decade / no earlier than 2030.

evidence.name: CARIOQA quantum space gravimetry pathfinder
evidence.detail: Phase A completed June 2025; Phase B kicked off 15–16 October 2025 (24 months) to raise payload and platform technologies to TRL 6. Single accelerometer pathfinder, not a gradiometer.

concepts.name: Intensity interferometry of sunlit orbital objects
concepts.physics: Hanbury Brown–Twiss: intensity fluctuations at two apertures are correlated by |γ|², the squared degree of coherence, which encodes angular structure. Only nanosecond timing is needed, not optical phase stability, so baselines of kilometers between free-flyers are feasible.
concepts.application: Angular characterization of GEO objects from their solar glint; stellar astrometry. Earth-surface imaging is not viable because the source is not hot and bright enough.
concepts.failure: SNR scales with the square of the source brightness temperature and needs large photon rates; ground demos on stars took hours.
concepts.first: Photon rate from a glinting GEO satellite at a 1 m aperture and the integration time to reach |γ|² SNR of 5.
concepts.prior: Intensity-correlation imaging of sunlit GEO satellites has been studied since an AFRL-funded Texas A&M telescope reached first light on a star in 2008, with a pessimistic SNR analysis by Fried, Riker and Agrawal (JOSA A 2014){R449} and design studies by Hyland (Appl. Opt. 2024){R450}; a free-flying space intensity interferometer for stars was analysed by Klein, Guelman and Lipson (Appl. Opt. 2007){R451}. No satellite has been imaged this way. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground stellar intensity interferometry proves the physics{R452}{R453}.

evidence.name: Stellar intensity interferometry
evidence.instrument: Narrabri-type and VERITAS photon-counting intensity interferometers
evidence.operator: Hanbury Brown & Twiss (Jodrell Bank, 1956); VERITAS collaboration (2020)
evidence.detail: Angular diameter of Sirius measured by intensity correlation in 1956; four-telescope stellar intensity interferometry demonstrated with VERITAS in 2020.

evidence.name: Intensity-correlation imaging of GEO satellites (SNR and design studies)
evidence.detail: SNR limitations for sunlit GEO objects analysed (pessimistic); 2024 design for geostationary satellite inspection. No satellite imaged.

evidence.name: Space-based intensity interferometer (free-flyers)
evidence.detail: Concept and formation-flying analysis for a stellar intensity interferometer in space.

concepts.name: Entanglement-assisted long-baseline optical imaging
concepts.physics: Gottesman–Jennewein–Croke (2012): a shared entangled photon pair lets two apertures interfere incoming light without physically transporting it between them, using a teleportation-style measurement{R455}. Removes the beam-transport loss that makes optical VLBI impossible.
concepts.application: Centimeter-scale resolution from GEO or beyond; the end-state for passive optical resolution limits.
concepts.failure: Entangled-pair rates must match the incoming photon rate per mode; quantum memories and repeaters at telescope scale do not exist; decades out.
concepts.first: Required entangled-pair rate for a given target photon flux and baseline.
concepts.prior: The scheme is Gottesman, Jennewein and Croke (PRL 2012){R455}; tabletop and 20 km fibre demonstrations on simulated thermal sources followed (Brown et al. 2023{R456}; Wang et al., USTC 2025, preprint){R457}, and a 2018 IAC conference paper (La Mura et al.) proposed entanglement-sharing space telescope arrays{R458}. No funded space study, mission or on-sky starlight demonstration found; the orbital application is an extrapolation of published work. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Theory and tabletop experiments.

evidence.name: Entanglement-assisted interferometric imaging (tabletop)
evidence.instrument: SPDC entangled photon pairs, pseudo-thermal source
