evidence.detail: Simulated thermal source imaged by interfering collected light with shared entangled modes and joint measurement; first lab implementation of the GJC scheme.

evidence.name: Memory-assisted nonlocal interferometer over 20 km fibre
evidence.instrument: two cold-atom-ensemble quantum memories (DLCZ), quantum frequency conversion, field-deployed fibre
evidence.detail: Simulated thermal light measured with a fibre-link baseline up to 20 km and 1.5 km geometric-delay compensation; nodes in a single laboratory. Preprint only.

evidence.name: Longer-baseline telescopes using quantum repeaters (theory)
evidence.detail: Theoretical scheme; space telescope-array variants proposed at IAC 2018.

concepts.name: Infrasound-in-airglow impulsive-event monitoring
concepts.physics: Explosions and large impulsive events launch infrasound and acoustic-gravity waves that reach 85–95 km within minutes and modulate OH and O airglow brightness by percent-level amounts.
concepts.application: A GEO airglow imager at high cadence becomes a passive global monitor for nuclear tests, volcanic explosions and large accidents, with arrival-time triangulation.
concepts.failure: Discriminating impulsive signatures from the dense background of gravity waves; nighttime only for most emissions; cloud contamination for nadir viewing.
concepts.first: Expected airglow modulation amplitude vs source yield and distance, against imager noise at 1 s cadence.
concepts.prior: Ground imagers and GOLD/ICON see gravity waves{R459}{R460}{R461}; a dedicated impulsive-event system has not flown as far as I know.
concepts.trlNote: Hunga Tonga (2022) acoustic-gravity waves were seen in airglow from ground and from GOLD/ICON{R462}{R459}{R460}{R461}.

evidence.name: Ground airglow imaging of Hunga Tonga acoustic-gravity waves
evidence.detail: Multiple eruption- and tsunami-generated wave packets observed in mesopause OH airglow (~87 km) over China.

evidence.name: GOLD and ICON observations of Hunga Tonga waves
evidence.instrument: GOLD far-ultraviolet imager (GEO, SES-14); ICON MIGHTI
evidence.detail: GOLD saw >100 K wave-like thermospheric temperature perturbations (300–400 m/s, >2400 km wavelength); ICON MIGHTI measured extreme neutral winds. Operational airglow instruments not designed for impulsive-event monitoring; no dedicated high-cadence GEO monitor flown.

concepts.name: Orbital magnetotelluric sounding of the crust
concepts.physics: Natural ionospheric current variations induce currents in the conductive Earth; the ratio of induced to inducing field vs period gives conductivity vs depth. Swarm has done this at mantle scale{R463}{R464}{R465}.
concepts.application: Regional crustal conductivity for geothermal and mineral targeting; basin-scale resistivity where no ground MT exists.
concepts.failure: Spatial resolution scales with altitude; crustal-scale needs a very low orbit (drag) or dense swarms; separating the induced field from ionospheric source structure.
concepts.first: Resolution vs altitude for a 3-satellite swarm at 250 km with 0.1 nT magnetometers.
concepts.prior: Mantle-scale induction from Swarm published{R463}{R464}{R465}; crustal-scale would be new.
concepts.trlNote: Mantle-scale induction from Swarm published{R463}{R464}{R465}.

evidence.name: Swarm satellite electromagnetic induction sounding of the mantle
evidence.instrument: Swarm vector field magnetometers (with CryoSat-2 and observatories)
evidence.operator: ESA Swarm; analyses by LPG Nantes, ETH Zurich, DTU
evidence.detail: Mantle conductivity profiles and 3-D structure recovered from Swarm magnetospheric and tidal signals; depth sensitivity is mantle-scale (hundreds of km); crustal-scale induction not attempted.

concepts.name: Brillouin lidar for ocean temperature profiles
concepts.physics: Spontaneous Brillouin backscatter in water is shifted by ~7–8 GHz, proportional to sound speed, which is dominated by temperature. A narrow-linewidth green lidar with an edge-filter or heterodyne receiver returns a temperature profile through the top tens of meters.
concepts.application: Mixed-layer temperature structure, which satellites currently see only at the skin; ocean heat content and hurricane fuel.
concepts.failure: Brillouin cross-section is small and the water column attenuates; from orbit the photon budget is marginal at best. Likely lives on aircraft.
concepts.first: Photons per shot per 5 m depth bin from 500 km with a 1 m aperture and 1 J pulses.
concepts.prior: Laboratory profiling to 0.07 °C and 1 m was demonstrated by Rudolf and Walther (Opt. Eng. 2014){R466}. The US Navy funded a Brillouin ocean-temperature lidar aimed at airborne use (BOLTS, SBIR N211-089, 2022–2025), which reached a water-tank prototype with ocean testing planned{R467}{R468}, NASA Langley published an airborne receiver concept (2024){R469} and NASA Goddard ran observing-system simulations for ocean heat content (Remote Sensing 2024){R470}. No spaceborne instrument or satellite photon-budget study found; the airborne step this entry expected is funded but not yet demonstrated. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Laboratory demonstrations; no peer-reviewed shipboard result was found (checked 2026-11-04){R466}.

evidence.name: Brillouin lidar with atomic (ESFADOF) edge-filter receiver
evidence.instrument: Frequency-doubled pulsed fibre-amplifier lidar, water-tank range
evidence.detail: Real-time remote temperature profiles in a laboratory water column from the spontaneous Brillouin shift; accuracy about 0.07 °C with about 1 m depth resolution.

evidence.name: BOLTS (Brillouin Ocean LiDAR Technology System)
evidence.instrument: High-spectral-resolution, range-gated blue/green lidar measuring Brillouin shift and linewidth
evidence.operator: Areté Associates under ONR SBIR topic N211-089 (contract N68335-22-C-0622)
evidence.detail: Navy transition quad chart shows laboratory testing with a seawater fixture (TRL 4, Q4 FY24) and planned ocean testing (TRL 5, Q2 FY25); requirement: sound speed to 1.5 m/s, 5 m along-beam resolution, 40 m range in mesotrophic water. No public report of the ocean test found.

evidence.name: Brillouin asymmetric spatial heterodyne (BASH) lidar receiver concept
evidence.instrument: BASH spectrometer receiver for airborne ocean lidar
evidence.detail: Conceptual receiver for depth-resolved temperature, salinity and sound-velocity profiles from aircraft; sensitivity analysis and lidar simulations only.

evidence.name: Ocean temperature profiling lidar OSSE
evidence.instrument: Simulated Brillouin lidar against ECCOv4r4 ocean model
evidence.detail: Observing-system simulations of upper-ocean heat storage retrieval; measurement errors of a real Brillouin lidar not included.

concepts.name: Umbra-station limb transmission spectroscopy
concepts.physics: Earth's umbra extends ~1.4 million km anti-sunward. A spectrometer inside it sees the Sun fully eclipsed with a refracted ring of limb-transmitted light: a continuous all-longitude transmission spectrum through roughly 100× the airmass of a nadir sounder.
concepts.application: Trace-gas limb profiles integrated around the whole terminator; Earth as an exoplanet analog for transit-spectroscopy validation.
concepts.failure: Station-keeping deep in the umbra; the ring is faint and refraction-limited below ~10 km tangent height; limited to terminator geometry by construction.
concepts.first: Ring radiance vs tangent height and the spectral resolution achievable with a 20 cm telescope.
concepts.prior: Mayorga et al. (PSJ 2021) proposed a small satellite beyond the Earth–Sun L2 point to observe Earth transiting the Sun in transmission at 0.2–2.5 µm{R471}; that vantage lies past the umbra tip, so it is a transit rather than this umbral refracted-ring geometry. Earth's limb transmission spectrum has otherwise been measured through lunar eclipses from the ground (Pallé et al. 2009){R472} and from HST (Youngblood et al. 2020){R473}, and Kaguya imaged the refracted ring from lunar orbit in 2009{R474}. No spectrometer stationed inside the umbra has been proposed. Checked 2026-10-17.

evidence.name: Earth-transit transmission spectroscopy satellite beyond Sun–Earth L2
evidence.operator: Johns Hopkins APL and collaborators (Mayorga et al.)
evidence.detail: Modelled Earth transmission spectra during transits of the Sun including solar and planetary variability; concluded a satellite beyond L2 is needed. Transit geometry, not the umbral refracted-ring geometry of this entry.

evidence.name: Earth limb transmission spectrum via lunar eclipse
evidence.instrument: Ground telescopes (2008 eclipse) and HST/STIS (January 2019 eclipse)
evidence.operator: Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias; NASA/STScI
evidence.detail: Transmission spectrum of Earth's atmosphere recovered from eclipsed moonlight; O3, O2, H2O and Rayleigh features identified in the optical, near-UV featureless due to strong O3 absorption. Demonstrates the limb-transmission measurement but from the Moon's position, not inside the umbra.

evidence.name: Kaguya (SELENE) HDTV imaging of Earth's sunlit atmospheric ring
evidence.detail: Incidental imaging from lunar orbit of the Sun almost fully occulted by Earth during the 10 Feb 2009 (JST) penumbral lunar eclipse, showing the backlit atmospheric ring; imagery only, no spectroscopy.

concepts.name: Cosmic-ray radio pulses as impulsive illuminators
concepts.physics: Extensive air showers emit nanosecond broadband radio pulses (30–1000 MHz) via geomagnetic and Askaryan mechanisms. The ANITA balloon detected these reflected off the Antarctic ice sheet; the reflection's polarity and amplitude encode surface reflectivity and near-surface density.
concepts.application: Passive VHF/UHF ground-penetrating radar of ice sheets with nature's transmitter; potentially firn density and surface roughness.
concepts.failure: Event rate above threshold is low; the source position must be reconstructed per event; SNR at orbital altitude vs balloon altitude.
concepts.first: Rate of showers above 10¹⁸ eV per day within the footprint, and received field strength at 500 km.
concepts.prior: ANITA detected ice-reflected cosmic-ray radio pulses (Hoover et al., PRL 2010){R475}; Antarctic surface reflectivity was measured from the same payload with the Sun and a balloon pulser rather than cosmic rays (Besson et al., Radio Science 2015; Gorham et al. 2017){R476}{R477}; a JPL satellite concept (SWORD, 2013, preprint only) studied orbital detection of the reflected pulses for cosmic-ray science{R478}; Shoemaker et al. (Ann. Glaciol. 2020) read anomalous ANITA events as subsurface firn reflections{R479}. No work uses the showers as a systematic illuminator for ice-sheet sensing. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: ANITA incidental detections serve as proof of concept{R475}.

evidence.name: ANITA-1 detection of ice-reflected UHECR radio pulses
evidence.operator: ANITA collaboration / NASA Long Duration Balloon program
evidence.detail: 16 ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray air-shower radio events observed, mostly via reflection off the Antarctic ice sheet, identified by inverted polarity relative to direct events.

evidence.name: Antarctic surface RF reflectivity from ANITA with the Sun and the HiCal balloon pulser
evidence.instrument: ANITA-II/-III receivers; HiCal-1 companion pulser balloon
evidence.detail: Power reflection coefficients of the ice surface measured as a function of incidence angle using solar radio emission (consistent with Fresnel) and a balloon-borne pulser (200–600 MHz departure from Fresnel attributed to roughness and clutter).

evidence.name: SWORD (Synoptic Wideband Orbiting Radio Detector)
evidence.detail: Concept study of LEO detection of surface-reflected UHECR radio pulses for cosmic-ray science (~100 events/yr above 10^20 eV); addresses ionospheric dispersion. Not funded or flown.

evidence.name: Subsurface firn reflection interpretation of anomalous ANITA events
evidence.operator: Shoemaker et al. (Virginia Tech, UCLA, Utrecht, JPL, Stanford, Imperial)
evidence.detail: Shows that subsurface density layers in Antarctic firn could produce non-inverted reflected events, i.e., the reflected pulses carry near-surface structure information.

concepts.name: Rotational Doppler via orbital-angular-momentum beams
concepts.physics: A beam carrying OAM ℓ reflected from a surface rotating at Ω acquires a frequency shift ℓΩ/π, independent of translational Doppler. Measures spin state directly.
concepts.application: Tumble rate of debris; reaction-wheel and rotor signatures of satellites; non-cooperative attitude determination.
concepts.failure: OAM beams need to overfill the target and preserve mode structure; divergence rules out ground targets from orbit; viable only at satellite-to-satellite ranges.
concepts.first: Mode purity after propagation to 100 km and the required target size for a given ℓ.
concepts.prior: Demonstrated in the laboratory by Lavery et al. (Science 2013){R480} and extended to rough surfaces and free-space ranges by Chinese groups (Opt. Express 2022 and later){R481}, with several papers treating non-cooperative rotating targets, tilt, offset and precession{R482}{R483}. No proposal or demonstration of satellite-to-satellite spin measurement of orbital objects found. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Laboratory demonstrations{R480}.

evidence.name: Rotational Doppler shift from a spinning rough surface with OAM light
evidence.detail: Frequency shift proportional to ℓΩ observed in light scattered from a rotating rough surface, independent of the surface being a specular reflector.

evidence.name: Free-space remote rotational-Doppler detection with a combined vortex beam
evidence.instrument: Coherently combined vortex probe beam, outdoor free-space path
evidence.operator: Central South University and collaborators (Yu, Xie et al.)
evidence.detail: First demonstration of the rotational Doppler effect from a rotating rough surface using a coherently combined vortex beam over a free-space path; range reported as about 1 km in secondary sources (not confirmed from the abstract).

evidence.name: Rotational Doppler velocimetry at oblique incidence and large tilt
evidence.operator: Harbin Institute of Technology and others
evidence.detail: Spectral broadening from tilt and misalignment analysed and compensated, extending measurement to tilt angles up to about 70 degrees — the non-cooperative-target case.

concepts.name: Ground laser guide star as calibrated overhead target
concepts.physics: A ground site excites a sodium-layer beacon at 90 km; a LEO imager views it from above. The result is a point source of known altitude, brightness and position, with the entire troposphere removed from the path.
concepts.application: MTF, geolocation and radiometric cross-calibration of commercial imagers; a second beacon gives a known baseline for stereo and pointing calibration.
concepts.failure: Beacon brightness from above is marginal for a 30 cm aperture at a 1 ms line time (SNR about 4) and comfortable from 50 cm up; radiometry needs a stare of order a second. The return is a single 589 nm line, so radiometric cross-calibration covers one band only. Scheduling against existing LGS sites; daylight operation impossible.
concepts.first: Beacon irradiance at 500 km for a 20 W laser and the resulting SNR for a 30 cm imager at 1 ms exposure.
concepts.prior: Psiaki, Flewelling and Hackett (NAVIGATION 2019) proposed that an orbiting camera observe a network of ground-pumped sodium guide stars as known-position references for autonomous orbit determination{R484}, the closest published use of a mesospheric beacon viewed from above. Ground lasers aimed directly at satellites have been used or patented for radiometric and polarisation calibration (NASA GSLC, 2014–2015){R485}{R486} and geolocation alignment (GOES-R GLM ground beacons, 2017–2018){R487}; Ball Aerospace patented a spacecraft-generated sodium guide star for adaptive-optics wavefront correction (2001){R488}. No use of a ground LGS for MTF or radiometric calibration of a LEO imager found. Physics entirely off-the-shelf. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: First calculation run 2026-10-17 (scripts/calc/c17_laser_guide_star.py). A 20 W CW sodium laser returns about 10⁷ photons s⁻¹ m⁻² to a ground telescope, matching published returns{R489}, and 5×10⁵ photons s⁻¹ m⁻² at 410 km slant range. A 30 cm imager detects about 17 photons per 1 ms line, SNR 4, against negligible background through a 1 nm filter; 50 cm gives SNR 7 and 1 m gives 14. Centroiding and MTF work at the line rate with TDI; 1 % radiometry needs about 0.6 s of staring. TRL 3 on the analytic link budget; every component remains TRL 9.

evidence.name: Ground laser guide star as calibrated overhead target — link budget
evidence.instrument: 20 W cw sodium laser beacon viewed by a 30 cm–1 m LEO imager (analysis)
evidence.detail: Analytic photon budget using published sodium return fluxes (about 10^7 photons s^-1 m^-2 at the ground for a 20 W cw laser) scaled to 410 km slant range; SNR 4–14 per 1 ms line for 30 cm–1 m apertures.

evidence.name: Sodium guide-star network for autonomous orbit determination
evidence.instrument: Spacecraft camera plus star tracker observing ground-pumped sodium streaks (concept)
evidence.detail: Observability and Cramér–Rao analysis: seven or more independent streak observations determine a Keplerian orbit and clock offset; ~20 m 1-sigma position over several days. No hardware demonstration.

evidence.name: GOES-16 GLM geolocation validation with ground laser beacons
evidence.instrument: 777 nm pulsed laser beacons at two NASA satellite laser ranging stations observed by GLM from GEO
evidence.detail: Beacons mimicking lightning emission were detected by GLM; geolocation offsets from the surveyed beacon sites were within the 5 km requirement. Demonstrates a ground laser as a known-position target for an orbiting imager (not a mesospheric guide star).

evidence.name: Ground-to-space laser calibration (GSLC) method
evidence.instrument: Ground cw laser with controlled polarization and wavelength illuminating an on-orbit sensor
evidence.detail: Patented method for on-orbit polarization-sensitivity, degradation, spectral-response and stray-light calibration; the patents document the method, not an on-orbit demonstration.

evidence.name: Spacecraft-generated synthetic (sodium / Rayleigh) guide star for an Earth-viewing telescope
evidence.instrument: Spacecraft-mounted 589 nm beacon laser, deformable mirror and wavefront sensor (patent)
evidence.detail: Patent for adaptive-optics wavefront correction of a large on-orbit-assembled Earth-remote-sensing telescope using a laser beacon in the atmosphere; no flight.

concepts.name: Rayleigh–Brillouin lineshape lidar for temperature
concepts.physics: The spectral shape of molecular backscatter (Tenti S6 model){R490} depends on temperature and pressure independently of any Doppler shift. A high-resolution Fabry–Pérot or etalon receiver on a UV lidar resolves the lineshape.
concepts.application: Temperature profiles with no radiosonde-style prior; a natural add-on to any Aeolus successor.
concepts.failure: Requires resolving ~GHz-scale features with adequate photon counts; aerosol Mie contamination in the boundary layer.
concepts.first: Photon-limited temperature precision per 1 km bin from an Aeolus-class transmitter.
concepts.prior: Ground demonstrations and a 2021 airborne Rayleigh–Brillouin temperature retrieval on the DLR Falcon (Witschas et al., Opt. Lett. 2021); Aeolus used the Rayleigh channel for winds only{R491}{R492}.
concepts.trlNote: Ground and airborne (2021) Rayleigh–Brillouin lidar demos; the airborne retrieval argues for 5, left at 4 until a spaceborne photon budget is shown to close{R491}.

evidence.name: Ground-based UV Rayleigh–Brillouin temperature lidar
evidence.instrument: 354.9 nm lidar with Fabry–Pérot spectral filter scanned over the RB line (ALADIN airborne demonstrator technology on the ground)
evidence.detail: Daytime atmospheric temperature profiles from 2 to 15 km retrieved from the measured Rayleigh–Brillouin line shape.

evidence.name: ALADIN Airborne Demonstrator (A2D) RB temperature profiling
evidence.instrument: A2D UV lidar on the DLR Falcon, Fabry–Pérot spectral scan over 11 GHz
evidence.detail: First airborne daytime temperature profile (10.5 km down to about 1.4 km) from Rayleigh–Brillouin scattering over Iceland; 630 m vertical resolution, biases under ±2 K versus radiosonde and model, random error 0.1–0.4 K.

evidence.name: Aeolus / ALADIN Rayleigh channel
evidence.instrument: ALADIN 355 nm Doppler wind lidar, double-edge Fabry–Pérot Rayleigh receiver
evidence.detail: Spaceborne UV lidar with a Fabry–Pérot molecular-backscatter channel flown in LEO and operated for wind; the Tenti S6 line shape is used in the wind processor but temperature was not a mission product. Establishes the hardware heritage, not the temperature retrieval, from orbit.

concepts.name: Ku/Ka reflectometry from megaconstellation downlinks
concepts.physics: GNSS-R at L-band senses ~20 cm roughness. Starlink and OneWeb downlinks at 12–20 GHz are ~10× stronger and ~10× shorter wavelength, sensitive to cm-scale roughness. The same illuminators enable passive bistatic SAR.
concepts.application: Wind stress, thin-film sea-ice state, snow wetness, soil moisture at finer scales; passive imaging with no transmitter.
concepts.failure: Beam-steered downlinks illuminate only user cells; waveform knowledge is proprietary, so a reference channel is required; ITU and provider consent.
concepts.first: Fraction of ocean surface illuminated at any instant by a real constellation's beam plan.
concepts.prior: Ground demonstrations exist: Starlink-illuminated passive SAR images from a fixed receiver (Gomez-del-Hoyo and Samczynski, IEEE JSTARS 2024){R385} and Starlink/OneWeb signal characterisation for passive radar (Fraunhofer FHR, 2023){R494}{R495}. Ku-band bistatic sea-state retrieval was shown earlier with GEO DirecTV signals (Shah et al., IEEE TGRS 2016){R496}. No geophysical retrieval from megaconstellation reflections, no airborne demonstration and no orbital receiver were found. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Ground passive-radar imaging with Starlink signals (2024){R385} and Ku-band bistatic sea state from GEO signals (2016){R496} validate the components; TRL 4. The earlier airborne-demo claim did not survive a search.

evidence.name: Starlink-illuminated passive SAR demonstrator
evidence.instrument: Ground-based passive radar receiver using Starlink user-downlink (Ku-band) signals, back-projection imaging
evidence.detail: First Starlink-based passive SAR images of urban areas obtained under direct and adjacent-cell illumination from a fixed ground receiver.

evidence.name: SABBIA multichannel passive radar with Starlink / OneWeb illuminators
evidence.instrument: Tracking reference and surveillance antennas, wideband Ku-band receiver
evidence.detail: Recorded Starlink and OneWeb user-downlink signals; ambiguity-function analysis found both suitable as complementary illuminators of opportunity; multichannel demonstrator architecture for persistent bistatic SAR interferometry presented.

evidence.name: Ku-band (DirecTV) bistatic sea-state retrieval from signals of opportunity
evidence.instrument: Reflectometry receivers for GPS L-band, XM S-band and DirecTV Ku-band GEO signals
evidence.operator: Purdue University / NASA JPL and collaborators (Shah, Garrison et al.)
evidence.detail: Significant wave height retrieved from bistatic scattering of communication-satellite signals at L-, S- and Ku-band in field experiments; establishes geophysical retrieval at Ku-band from a GEO illuminator.

concepts.name: Lightning as a broadband in-atmosphere spectrometer source
concepts.physics: The lightning optical spectrum is known well enough{R497} that its appearance from space, after transit through cloud and the column above, encodes absorption. GLM images lightning in a single 1 nm band at the 777.4 nm oxygen triplet{R173}; the O2 A-band depth would add the altitude dimension.
concepts.application: Water vapor and aerosol above cloud, at the place and instant of deep convection where soundings are weakest.
concepts.failure: Multiple scattering inside cloud smears the path length; spectral variability of lightning itself; low light for hyperspectral at 500 fps.
concepts.first: Information content of a 20-band lightning spectrum for water vapor above cloud top, with scattering path-length uncertainty included.
concepts.prior: Single-band flown{R173}; multiband not.

evidence.name: Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM) single-band lightning imaging
evidence.instrument: GLM, 1372x1300 CCD, single ~1 nm band at 777.4 nm
evidence.detail: Operational single-band optical lightning imaging from GEO since GOES-16 (2017) establishes space detection of lightning emission in one atomic-oxygen line; no multiband or spectrometer instrument has flown and no published analysis of lightning-as-source absorption spectroscopy from space was found. Level entry is the closest permitted label for a flown heritage component supporting a TRL 2 concept.

evidence.name: Time-resolved lightning return-stroke optical spectrum
evidence.detail: Ground spectroscopy establishing the lightning emission spectrum (N II, O I, H-alpha lines and continuum) that the concept would use as a known source.

concepts.name: Laser-comm links as an aggregated turbulence and aerosol network
concepts.physics: Every satellite-to-ground laser link is a scintillometer: intensity variance and temporal spectrum give integrated Cn², and multi-aperture receivers give coarse profiles; mean loss gives aerosol extinction. Thousands of links are coming.
concepts.application: Global turbulence and aerosol climatology at no incremental cost; input to site selection and to optical-comm availability models.
concepts.failure: Adaptive optics and automatic gain control on operational links suppress the very signal being measured; data access from operators.
concepts.first: Which raw telemetry (pre-AGC power, tip-tilt residuals) an operator would need to expose.
concepts.prior: Characterized on individual links (OICETS, LCRD){R388}{R498}{R394}; nobody aggregates them as a sensing network, as far as I know.
concepts.trlNote: Individual-link characterization is the proof of concept{R388}{R394}.

evidence.name: OICETS (Kirari) ground-to-satellite laser links
evidence.instrument: NICT optical ground station to OICETS LUCE terminal, bidirectional 2006 campaign
evidence.detail: Uplink and downlink scintillation measured on real space-ground links, including dependence on number of transmitted beams and temporal frequency response; downlink scintillation index consistent with strong-fluctuation theory.

evidence.name: LCRD GEO-to-ground optical links
evidence.instrument: LCRD on STPSat-6 (GEO) with optical ground stations in California and Hawaii
evidence.operator: NASA Goddard / JPL / MIT Lincoln Laboratory
evidence.detail: Two-year experiment program (completed June 2024) included measurements of atmospheric optical channel effects (turbulence, weather) on link performance and availability; the downlink was also used as a reference beam for RINGSS turbulence profiling at Table Mountain, giving day/night Cn2 profiles and r0.

concepts.name: Thermal-infrared Stokes polarimetry
concepts.physics: Emitted radiance from smooth surfaces is partially polarized by the Fresnel emissivity; degree and angle of linear polarization at LWIR give surface roughness and refractive index, and distinguish oil films, wet vs dry, and man-made vs natural.
concepts.application: Night, no-illumination material discrimination; oil-spill detection independent of sun glint.
concepts.failure: Instrument polarization and calibration at LWIR are hard; degree of polarization is only a few percent for most natural surfaces.
concepts.first: Expected degree of polarization vs view angle for water, oil and soil at 10 µm, against a realistic polarimetric accuracy.
concepts.prior: Balloon (2021) and ground demonstrations; no peer-reviewed fixed-wing airborne Stokes polarimeter and no orbital LWIR polarimeter were found (checked 2026-11-04){R499}{R500}.
concepts.trlNote: A stratospheric-balloon LWIR spectro-polarimeter (2021) and outdoor ground tests; TRL 5 rests on the balloon flight{R499}{R500}.

evidence.name: Infrared Channeled Spectro-Polarimeter (IRCSP) balloon flight
evidence.operator: University of Arizona / NASA Goddard (CSBF balloon)
evidence.detail: High-altitude flight from the Columbia Scientific Balloon Facility, August 2021; linear polarization of cloud tops measured, degree of linear polarization from about 1 % to 20 %.

evidence.name: LWIR polarization oil-spill detection system (airborne-intended)
evidence.instrument: Long-wave infrared polarization imaging equipment with polarization-maintaining optics
evidence.operator: Changchun University of Science and Technology and collaborators (Sun et al.)
evidence.detail: Outdoor controlled tests on crude oil, palm oil, gasoline and diesel over seawater; polarization-degree images show more than 3 % contrast and separate oil types indistinguishable in intensity. Abstract reports outdoor tests, not flight data.

concepts.name: Quantum illumination / quantum radar
concepts.physics: Entangled signal–idler pairs improve target detection in noise by up to 6 dB in error exponent at low signal-to-noise{R502}{R503}. The advantage requires retaining the idler and shrinks with loss.
concepts.application: Claimed: low-observable target detection.
concepts.failure: The advantage evaporates over kilometers of propagation loss and at microwave frequencies where thermal photons dominate; no path to orbital ranges.
concepts.first: None recommended; treat as killed unless a new mechanism appears.
concepts.prior: Laboratory demonstrations only: about 1 dB advantage in an on-chip cryogenic microwave experiment (Assouly et al., Nature Physics 2023){R504}. Independent analyses converge on a power-limited range ceiling: Shapiro's own review (IEEE AES Magazine 2020){R505}, Jonsson and Ankel (IEEE RadarConf 2021){R506}, and Pavan and Galati (Remote Sensing 2024), who put the intrinsic range for aircraft-class targets below 1 km and typically tens of metres{R507}. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Lab demos at metre scale{R504}. Physics-dubious at orbital ranges: the sub-photon-per-mode power ceiling caps range at well under 1 km in every published analysis, including the protocol originator's{R505}{R506}{R507}.

evidence.name: Microwave quantum-illumination (quantum radar) experiment with superconducting circuits
evidence.instrument: Josephson-circuit entangled signal-idler source and cryogenic receiver
evidence.detail: Quantum advantage over the optimal classical illumination demonstrated in a cryogenic microwave setup (journal version of the 2022 arXiv experiment); sub-1 dB-class advantage in a laboratory geometry.

evidence.name: Range analyses of microwave quantum radar
evidence.operator: MIT (Shapiro); Saab / Chalmers (Jonsson, Ankel); Tor Vergata (Pavan, Galati)
evidence.detail: Independent analyses conclude that the low-brightness (sub-photon-per-mode) regime required for quantum advantage limits range for aircraft-class targets to under about 1 km and typically tens of metres; classical noise radar outperforms by orders of magnitude.

concepts.name: Synthetic-aperture lidar from LEO
concepts.physics: Aperture synthesis at 1 µm would give centimeter resolution from GEO in principle; it needs phase knowledge to λ/8 (~130 nm) across the synthetic aperture.
concepts.application: Claimed: SAR-class all-weather-independent resolution at optical wavelengths.
concepts.failure: Orbital motion compensation to 130 nm over the synthetic-aperture time is far beyond current navigation; atmospheric phase screens decorrelate in milliseconds. Airborne SAL worked over short paths.
concepts.first: Required motion-compensation accuracy vs available ephemeris and a reference-return scheme; if it cannot close by 10×, stop.
concepts.prior: Airborne SAL (Krause et al., CLEO 2011) remains the only flight demonstration{R508}; orbital SAL and ISAL exist only in simulation (Shen et al., Aerospace 2025){R509}. Published analyses limit the synthetic aperture to the atmospheric coherence length (Karr, JOSA A 2003; Sensors 2008; refined by Schumm and Dierking, JOSA A 2017){R510}{R511}{R512}. The most optimistic long-range study (Gao and Dong, Sensors 2024, about 3000 km with coherence compensation) concerns ISAL of space objects with no atmospheric path{R513}. Checked 2026-10-17.
concepts.trlNote: Airborne SAL (2011) validates optical aperture synthesis{R508}; orbital motion compensation unaddressed and the atmosphere caps the aperture at its coherence length{R512}{R511}. Physics-dubious for Earth-looking SAL from LEO.

evidence.name: Airborne synthetic aperture ladar flight demonstration
evidence.detail: First reported airborne synthetic-aperture ladar images, validating optical aperture synthesis with aircraft motion compensation.

evidence.name: Space-based ISAL observation-mode analysis
evidence.instrument: STK-based simulation of space-based inverse SAL imaging GEO and LEO objects
evidence.operator: Shen et al. (Chinese Academy of Sciences institutes)
evidence.detail: Fly-around and fly-by imaging modes evaluated for minimum imaging time, PRF and SNR; simulation only, no hardware or flight.

evidence.name: Turbulence limits on synthetic aperture ladar
evidence.operator: Karr (2003); Guo et al. (2008); Schumm & Dierking, AFIT (2017)
evidence.detail: Atmospheric turbulence caps usable synthetic aperture near the SAL coherence length (Karr, Guo); wave-optics simulations find phase effects dominate amplitude by an order of magnitude and refine the simple coherence-length rule (Schumm & Dierking).

evidence.name: Long-range ISAL constraint analysis (space targets)
evidence.detail: Fibre lasers suffice to 22 km uncompensated; coherence compensation needed to 57 km; pulsed solid-state lasers with compensation analysed to about 3000 km for space situational awareness, i.e., no atmospheric path.

sun|dopp.text: Sunlight reflected from Earth targets: 1 m/s is Δλ/λ ≈ 3×10⁻⁹, three orders of magnitude below Fraunhofer line widths. Filled only for the Sun as its own target (helioseismology).

sun|phase.text: Sunlight's spatial coherence area at Earth is tens of micrometers; target-side phase is unusable. Coherence across apertures (HBT correlation, C09) or quantum-projected interference (C10) is the only route.

sun|tof.text: No time reference in sunlight. Ruled out.

sun|emis.text: Emission from the target is by definition not the Sun as source; see Earth emission row.

earth|tof.text: Thermal emission carries no timing. Ruled out.

earth|phase.text: Thermal emission is incoherent at the target; phase is exploited only across apertures (aperture synthesis, T23 and T76), which the receiver axis captures.

earth|inel.text: Inelastic processes need a pump; Earth's thermal field pumps nothing observable. Ruled out.

earth|refr.text: Refraction bends limb-emission ray paths and is modeled as a correction. Whether refraction of emitted radiation carries independent information is unexplored.

earth|escat.text: Scattering of thermal photons by clouds and aerosol is part of every radiative-transfer model (e.g. cirrus retrievals) but not exploited as a standalone observable.

earth|abs.text: Filled via sounders: the absorbing gas is also the emitter.

own|emis.text: A transmitter does not make the target emit unless via laser-induced processes, which belong to the inelastic column.

own|refl.text: Radar and lidar returns are classified as elastic scattering here; specular reflection (calm water, retroreflectors) is a special case of the same column.

own|abs.text: Differential absorption lidar is the flown case; laser occultation (C05) extends it.

own|pen.text: Earth subsurface sounding from orbit is blocked by the ionosphere below ~10 MHz; the planetary sounders show what an ionosphere-free body permits.

soo|inel.text: Opportunistic sources lack the power density for fluorescence or Raman. Ruled out.

soo|fieldc.text: GNSS signals sense the ionosphere via refraction and Faraday rotation, not the field directly. A field-coupling observable from signals of opportunity is unexplored.

soo|refl.text: Reflectometry is classified under elastic scattering; the specular component is reflection in the narrow sense.

transient|escat.text: Lightning RF scattered from the ionosphere is observed incidentally (T36). No dedicated use.

transient|dopp.text: Doppler of lightning RF from ionospheric motion is measurable in principle; no technique recalled.

transient|pol.text: Lightning RF polarization after ionospheric transit encodes Faraday rotation; unexplored as a technique.

transient|phase.text: No phase reference for a natural impulsive source. Ruled out.

transient|tof.text: Multi-satellite TDOA on lightning sferics is done at ground level (WWLLN){R514}{R515}; a space-based version is unexplored.

transient|fieldc.text: Lightning-driven electron precipitation (LEP) couples to the magnetic field; observed in situ, not used as a remote technique.

cosmic|emis.text: Quasar and pulsar emission is the source; the cell is filled via VLBI and pulsar timing under phase and time of flight.

cosmic|dopp.text: No Doppler observable of an Earth target from a cosmic source. Ruled out.

cosmic|pol.text: Stellar or CMB polarization passing through the atmosphere is essentially unchanged; unexplored and probably empty for good reason.

cosmic|pen.text: Cosmic-ray muons penetrate rock but the detector must lie beneath the target (muography); from orbit only gamma and neutron leakage from the top meter is accessible, and only on airless bodies.

cosmic|refl.text: Air-shower radio pulses reflected off ice (C15) are the only candidate.

field|refl.text: Fields do not reflect. Ruled out.

field|refr.text: Gravitational lensing by Earth is ~10⁻⁹ rad; unusable. Ruled out.

field|pol.text: Zeeman polarization of emission lines (T16, T25) couples field and polarization; classified under those rows.

field|phase.text: Inter-satellite ranging (T58) and atom interferometry (C08) use phase as the readout of field coupling.

field|tof.text: Chronometric geodesy (C07) is time as the field observable: clock rate vs geopotential.

field|pen.text: Magnetotelluric induction (C12) is the penetrating case.

earth|refl.text: Downwelling atmospheric emission reflected by the surface is the (1−ε) term in every land-surface-temperature and microwave sea-surface retrieval: a correction that is modeled and removed, not an observable anyone retrieves. Whether the reflected component carries independent information (surface reflectance in the thermal IR, cloud-base emission mirrored by water) is unexplored from orbit.

transient|refl.text: Lightning and bolide light reaches orbit by multiple scattering through cloud (T33, T34), which the grid files under emission and absorption, not reflection. Specular reflection of a transient's light from water, ice or the sea surface would give an independent geometry on the source; no technique recalled uses it.

transient|inel.text: Filled via T35: sprites, elves and halos are nitrogen emission excited by the lightning electromagnetic pulse and quasi-static field{R188}{R189}{R185}, a secondary emission pumped by the transient, counted here as inelastic by the same logic that files sounders under both emission and absorption. TGFs themselves are bremsstrahlung{R198}{R192} and stay under emission.

filters.name: Photon budget
filters.text: The solid angle of a 1 m² aperture from 500 km is ~4×10⁻¹² sr. Any inelastic process (Raman, Brillouin, fluorescence) must clear roughly 10 detected photons per resolution cell after yield × aperture × dwell. Brillouin lidar (C13) is marginal; Raman from orbit is not viable.

filters.name: Coherence vs platform motion
filters.text: LEO moves 7.5 km/s. Coherent optical techniques need phase stability to λ/8 over the integration time, which limits coherent integration to microseconds without a reference return. Vibrometry (C02) and synthetic-aperture lidar (C24) live or die here.

filters.name: Diffraction and baseline
filters.text: Resolving centimeters from GEO at visible wavelengths needs ~100 m apertures or synthesized baselines. Intensity interferometry (C09) and entanglement-assisted imaging (C10) are the only routes and both are photon-starved.

filters.name: Illumination geometry
filters.text: Signals-of-opportunity concepts (C05, C15, C19) hinge entirely on where transmitters, tangent points and receivers align. An orbital-geometry sweep is the first analysis, before any link budget.

interactionNote: Classification conventions used throughout: reflection is the geometric-optics regime (reflector much larger than λ, surface-bound); elastic scattering covers particles, volumes and rough surfaces where the return depends on the size parameter, so radar and lidar backscatter sit there. Sounders that invert thermal emission through an absorbing gas are counted under both emission and absorption. Techniques that exploit phase only across apertures (aperture synthesis) are filed under emission with a correlation receiver, not under phase, which is reserved for cases where phase is itself the observable.
